review:
Knowing that the Aeneid is referencing Homeric poems that were ancient in its time, I’m able to treat it as fan fiction. It feels modern because it is referencing ancient texts, and recasting them in a contemporary light.

The most interesting part of the poem to me: The Aeneid was used by Augustus to legitimize emperor rule, as well as to act as a unifying text or ideology to justify Rome's rule over the vast empire it had. It did, in fact, seem to achieve these goals.

But the poem itself retains an undercurrent of questioning the legitimacy of empire. Even an ambiguous poem can be effective as propaganda Like how people watch the Wolf of Wall Street as lionizing Jordan Belfort, even if when you watch the movie you’re like “wow this is horrible”.

title: The Path to Power (The Years of Lyndon Johnson, #1)
author: Robert A. Caro
review:
The first of a 5 part biography about LBJ. Podcaster Dwarkesh Patel claimed that these are perhaps the best books he's ever read (https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/lyndon-johnson). I was not disappointed.

I am still in the midst of reading these, (I am in the midst of the third book) and they feel like the best books I've ever read.

As gripping and as pic as any novel. But the story it tells is true.

Before I started reading this book, I sort of thought "how can someone really write a 4,000-page biography of one person? And have it all be interesting?"

The first chapter of the first book has 6 pages about the topography and ecology if the Texas Hill Country where LBJ grew up. All of it fascinating, and all of it truly important to the story Caro is telling about LBJ.

So that's how you can write 4,000 pages about one person.

Caro goes deep on the backstory of the people who interact with LBJ. He explains the details of how votes are counted in Texas elections.

Usually when I read history books, I make a ton of notes in the back of the book of questions I still have, things I want to look up to understand more. I have almost none with this book. No further questions. Any thread of interest, or dangling bit of uncertainty that in a lesser book would have prompted me to do further research has already been answered by Caro in beautiful and clear prose in the body of the book. There are almost no footnotes. All the facts, context, and setup you need flows in the body of the text.

Enough about the book itself. What about LBJ?

This first volume - 700 pages - book covers the time from Johnson's birth up until his time as a member of the House of Representatives, ad his first Senate race (which he lost) in 1941.

My first takeaway is how much of a lying liar Lyndon B Johnson was. He lied so much, so incessantly, and so shamelessly. Donald Trump lies a lot, but I bet LBJ lied more, even if only because it was harder to fact check people back then.

Lying was one of the many tools he used to accumulate power, which is what the book is really all about. He also used flattery, corruption, and verbal abuse. He did people favors and he stole votes. He had a vigorous work ethic, an attention to detail, and an keen eye to spot opportunities to create real value for others and aggregate power to himself in the process.

His ultimate aim in much of what he did - Caro convinces me - was to accumulate power in whatever way he could.

The paths available to him were not what you would call noble. But they were at least not violent. I am left with an appreciation that in order to accumulate his power, LBJ - while being as crooked a politician as can be - did actually have to make some people better off along the way. He was a good teacher in a poor Mexican school in south Texas, and as a high school debating coach in Houston. As a congressional secretary, he went out of his way over and over again to ensure his constituents were happy. He created jobs for many youths during the Great Depression as an able administrator of the National Youth Administration. As a Congressman he was largely responsible for his district in Texas getting electrified.

A great society is one where men without scruples like LBJ are forced, in their selfish pursuit of power, to create value for others along the way.

The fifth and final book of the biography, which covers most of his time as president, is not yet finished. That book will cover the twin legacies of Johnson's time as presidency: One for the good - his incredible legislative achievements with the Civil Rights Act and the Hart Cellar Immigration Act. And one for the bad - with the escalation of the US's presence in Vietnam. This twin legacy looms over the rest of this series, and I can't wait for Caro to finish that last book and for me to read it.

title: A History of Western Philosophy
author: Bertrand Russell
review:
Now one of my favorite history books ever!

Takes you from the ancient Greeks up to the 1940s, covering the major philosophical thinkers, one at a time. He mixes philosophical analysis of each thinker with enough history to put them in context. I think the balance is really good.

Russell evaluates philosophers largely by how much they contribute to or detract from the rise of science and liberalism. I like that he has a clear take. You have to have one to write a book like this - if the book tried to be totally objective then it would read like a wikipedia article and none of the facts would be "sticky".

One of my main takeaways from this book is how I am very much NOT a philosopher. A lot of philosophical disagreements just seem silly to me.

Another takeaway is just how wrong everyone is all the time. In one sense this is a "great man" theory of history book, because it is explicitly covering great and influential thinkers. But the fact that so many of these "great men" were flat-out wrong about so many things makes me take them off their pedestals.

Highly recommended if you are interested in big-picture history of ideas!

title: Two Paths to Prosperity: Culture and Institutions in Europe and China, 1000–2000
author: Avner Greif
review:
A compelling book about how different institutions evolved in China vs Europe.

Why do the Industrial Revolution happen in Europe? This is one of the many hooks trying to answer this question, and it is pretty good. May of the books (including others by Mokyr! I’m looking at you Culture of Growth) try to answer the question by only looking at Europe. These books fail because without a point comparison, the analysis is meaningless.

This book’s great strength is its comparative analysis. While undoubtably a big picture book, it focuses in on a few questions and answers the in detail for both China and Europe. Why did China and Europe develop different legal, governance, and social institutions between 1000-2000? And how do culture and institutions reinforce each other?

As a non specialist I’m not in a great position to evaluate the strength specific claims as to why Europe did great in the Industrial Revolution. It’s definitely plausible that communitarian values influence societal structure in a way that makes it harder to build inclusive politics and institutional competition needed to provide the groundwork for sustained innovation. We will never get a definitive answer as to why the Industrial Revolution happened in Europe, and even if we got one it’s not clear how valuable it would be. For one thing it would deprive half the historians of their jobs! But the grand theory in this book seems well worth considering (if you’re into that kind of thing) though with many grains of salt.

There are also many details of interest. For example:
- The administration of taxation was decentralized until the 1700s in Europe
- ⁠Social organization based on communitarian values means less need for institutions allowing impersonal trade. Eg no need for contract law, because contracts enforced by families.
- ⁠Lords were engaged in political process much more in Europe, by necessity because the state was fragmented. Europe had a tradition of councils that comes from Germanic councils and church synods
- ⁠Qing county courts were only active a few months ago year. Generally law in China had less reliance on courts of law
- less too was the reliance on a lawyerly class that has ⁠its devotion to the law as an abstract concept. Bailiffs held in higher esteem than their equivalent - the yamen (or runners) in China.
- ⁠European law is essentially a synthesis of Roman law, Catholic law, and German law.

title: The Rise and Fall of the EAST: How Exams, Autocracy, Stability, and Technology Brought China Success, and Why They Might Lead to Its Decline
author: Yasheng Huang
review:
A big picture book that argues that China's historical success is based on Exams, Autocracy, Stability and Technology.

The more of these kinds of models I come across, the more I think that the best of them are 50% right. If you want to be someone with a somewhat accurate and nuanced intellectual picture of history and politics, you need to be familiar with a lot of such models. But do you really want to be that kind of person?

Anyways, here are my takeaways:
- Westerners thought that technology would drive democracy. They were wrong.
- The exam system is fundamental to Chinese state power, and to Chinese culture. It pulls all the talented people into the state. Their ambitions are drawn towards the success of the state. This also means that they are not building civil society. This concentrates power in the state and supports autocracy.
- It also weakens the power of regional aristocrats.
- The exam system was rife with opportunities for favoritism. Graders could face powerful incentives to give high marks to the children of powerful people. Even something as small as the handwriting of the candidate could be used to signal the identity of the student to the grader. To combat this, all examinations (pages and pages of essays each) were hand copied by a set of 200-300 copyists.
- About half of juren - students receiving top marks on the exam - were the first person in their families to do so.
- The exam system had regional quotas to ensure that at least some people from disadvantaged provinces made it to the final rounds. Affirmative Action is not new.
- The Song dynasty - ~1000-1300 - saw the rise of neo-Confucianism which is much more statist than the original Confucianism.

I had known that Xi Jinping was doing a crackdown on corruption within the CCP, and consolidating his power to some extent. Specifically, he has:
- Purged corrupt party officials. This is good in its own right, and also gets rid of people who could challenge his power
- Less corruption also means more control
- Appointments are becoming more based on "integrity and loyalty" than merit
- He has enforced the rule that all companies must have an active CCP branch
- He has centralized some decision-making power from the state to the CCP

I was also keen to learn some specific potential action areas to for the US to build rapport with Chinese society.
- Demand reciprocal academic cooperation - if Chinse scholars come to the US, US scholars should also come to China. This will help drive more intellectual cooperation, as well as to promote better understanding.
- We can point out that incremental openness and respect for human rights are compatible with Chinese values (while not making unrealistic demands for full democracy).
- Intellectual appeals should be made to Chinese elites whose interest are harmed by the Chinese state.

title: The Royal Society: And the Invention of Modern Science
author: Adrian Tinniswood
review:
An ok, very short (129 page) introduction to the history of the Royal Society.

My takeaways:
- It is good for society when scientists to have prestige.
- That means we have to tolerate a degree of hobnobbery, elitism, status display, and politicking from scientists so that they can get the approval of people like The King. In more metaphorical language: "The key that opens treasures is often plain and rusty; but unless it be gilt, the key alone will make no shew at court."
- Profit motives drive discoveries: Many founders of the Society were interested in improvements to trade, commerce, and manufacturing. The first journal - Philosophical Transactions - was started by Henry Oldenburg in order to make a buck.
- The key to the society seems to have been immense curiosity - at times directed towards a profit motive - pursued in a manner that was remarkably well-managed.

Other bits of interest:
- Robert Hooke was employed full-time as a researcher by the societies - an early example of an institutional full-time research scientist.
- Cost of physical printing used to be a real barrier to dissemination of information. No longer.
- Newton's quote "If I have seen further, it is by standing on the shoulders of giants" was addressed to Hooke, who interpreted it as an insult to Hooke's short stature.

title: Civilization: The West and the Rest
author: Niall Ferguson
review:
How did countries in Western Europe come to dominate so much of the world? This is one of the most important questions in history. Ferguson's answer doesn't seem more wrong than anyone else's.

Ferguson claims that the West had 6 key characteristics that allowed it to dominate much of the rest of the world. Of those 6, I agree that 3 of them are really fundamental and important:
- Science. Clearly development of the scientific mode of reasoning allowed the west to make rapid progress in technology, and has led to us living much better lives than our ancestors
- Property rights. The system of private property gives people the right incentive to increase their productivity, produce surplus goods, which then raise the capabilities and power of their society (as well as standard of living).
- Competition: There were a lot of European countries competing with each other for resources and status. The strongest became quite strong, and when they extended their domain of competition to Africa/Asia/The Americas, the European powers were able to dominate the local societies.

His other 3 I don't really buy:
- Consumerism: I agree with his point that increasing productivity doesn't matter if you don't also have people wiling to pay to consume those goods. But I don't really buy that there was some orientation towards consumerism that fundamentally drove the west towards a more consumer-based society.
- Medicine: Obviously super important, but this is largely just downstream of science.
- Work ethic: Maybe, but I'm not convinced that this doesn't come largely from the competition and property dynamics.

Some of my other takeaways:
- No society is without downsides. One major downside that many societies in history have faced is that they did not provide the means for their citizens to grow their material wellbeing. (For most societies in history the child mortality rate was 50%+!).
- Western ideals, particularly economic and scientific ideas – are extremely powerful. The fact that many societies around the world are converging on them is not driven just by colonialism.
- For a while - including when this book was released - it looked like many countries were converging on western notions of property and freedom. But more recently this is not so clear.

title: On the Edge: The Art of Risking Everything
author: Nate Silver
review:
Incredibly fun.

He cuts elite society across the dimension of risk-seeking-ness, which combines a world I know fairly well (EA, rationalists, VCs) with a world I don't know at all (poker players, sports betters). He calls this collection of people "the river", and it is very interesting to see these groups compared with each other. He contrasts them with what he calls "the village" - government, academia, and media who are naturally not very risk-seeking.

A very interesting framework. Makes you think about how having different incentives towards risk will affect political views.

But the best part of the audiobook is how he does very mild impressions of everybody he quotes. His Peter Thiel sounds a lot like his ChatGPT. And you get just a hint of a Scottish accent when quotes Will MacAskill.

Maybe alarming how much I kept confusing Nate Silver for Michael Lewis while listening to this book. Especially when he was talking about Sam Bankman-Fried.

title: The Knowledge Machine: How Irrationality Created Modern Science
author: Michael Strevens
review:
I was quite convinced by the key arguments in this book, and it has changed how I think about science (as a field of human endeavor).

What is science? At it's core, it is is agreement that in formal scientific communication, the only accepted arguments will be those that are based on data.

Once people agree for data to be the basis of their arguments, then the rest of science follows. Data is all-important. We lock up researchers students for years as they generate and analyze data. We develop ever better and better measurement equipment, and better computers to help the researchers.

Science is a big complex apparatus to convince the brightest and most hardworking young people to devote the best years of their lives to sitting in rooms and collecting data on - for example - worms. Often boring, painstaking, laborious work that won't come to anything useful.

Because taken all together - all this data is incredibly useful.

Because it turns out that using evidence is a really incredible practical way to understand the world. It lets us cure diseases and build rocket ships and instantly talk to people across the world.

That basing our understanding on data is obvious to us who live in a post-science age. This was not at all obvious to pre-modern people.

(See how I remember what the book was about even as I write this review 6 months after reading it? Take notice Westad and Chen)

He's stretching things a bit when he tries to hammer home this point that science is "irrational" - but I don't really mind, and to me that isn't what the book is about.

title: The China Dream : The Elusive Quest for the Greatest Untapped Market on Earth

review:
Ignore the predictions about the future which are wrong (as they are in almost all books).

The useful parts of the book are to help understand why China successfully grew so much from the 1980s-200s.

My basic understanding after reading this book:
- China has a very stable government that is generally respected by its citizens. Why this is, I don't know, but this has been the case for thousands of years in China (except for the times between governments when the country is absolute chaos)
- That government was focused on driving economic growth
- And they had the support of the Western World, and the US in particular
- So they did it. The exact things they did are not crazy, but they just did them very well.
-- They developed light industry for exports
-- They attracted enormous amounts of foreign capital
-- They ensured that they got technology transfer along with that capital. They were able to do this because they are an attractive market to investors, and had a competent government invested in ensuring that in exchange for access to that market, they got good deals for their people

It has not always worked well for the companies that invested in China, who haven't gotten the returns they wanted, and haven't seen the level of deregulation that they expected. But it has undoubtedly worked out well for the Chinese people.

--

What about his predictions (which I told you to ignore)?

The book came out in 2002 and he says in his introduction that he thinks that China's recent success is "precursor to crisis" rather than "the harbringer of a new age". China kept up ~7-digit+ annual GDP per capita growth all the way until 2013. China's influence abroad - geopolitically, economically, culturally, have growth in the past 2 decades.

I don't really blame him for being wrong. People predicting geopolitics are almost always wrong. But I do blame him for trying.

title: Empires, Nations, and Families: A History of the North American West, 1800-1860
author: Anne F. Hyde
review:
Gives a nice feeling for the texture of life there and then, and I feel I leave it with a better understanding of the relationship between white settlers and native Americans at the time.

But I give it a low rating because there were a lot of detailed facts in the book - about individual people as well as overall historical events - but very few of them stuck with me. I'm not sure the exact problem - but I feel the book didn't have enough of an overall framework for me to be able to mentally organize and hang onto all the content.

Or maybe I was just bad at reading it.

title: The Hasidic Community of Williamsburg: A Study in the Sociology of Religion
author: Solomon Poll
review:
Fun to read about people who have such a radically different worldview to me!

The Hasidic Jews in Williamsburg are notable in comparison to other insular religious groups (e.g., Amish, Menonites) in that they live in a super dense suburban area with tons of distractions to potentially lure the youth away from the community - but they still maintain their values generation after generation.

Apparently, if you marry a non-Jew, it means that your family is now "defected" and none of your family members will be able to marry within the community.

Status in the group is given by level of religious observance.

But my favorite bit:
Observant Jews cannot work on the sabbath. And Hasidic Jews take an extremely wide definition "work".

Consider the following chain of events:
You open a walk-in refrigerator, causing warm air to come in
This causes the thermometer to rise, which in turns starts the motor to cool the refrigerator
Therefore you have - extremely indirectly - turned on the motor, which is a desecration of the Sabbath.

To get around this, a Hasidic Jew can install a timer on his fridge that turns the motor on and off at fixed intervals, irrespective of the door opening and closing. (Presumably the installation cannot happen on the Sabbath). Now the shop-owner can be assured that his fridge will be cold, and he does not have to worry that he is indirectly turning the motor on by opening the fridge.

This timer is marketed within the community as a "Sabbath Clock" - or a Fridge-O-Matic Zeiger:


"With the aid of God
Great Announcement
...
We announce that we have now perfected the Frig-O-Matic Sabbath Zeiger through which you may open the door of the refrigerator on the Sabbath every time and it doesn't make any difference whether the motor is running or in a standstill position.

The Frig-O-Matic Zeiger is refined in every respect, it is much nicer, smaller, and more practical, it is easier to regulate, and also it is cheaper, to make it possible for everyone to have one. It is completely automatic; once it is connected it is good for the Sabbath and for every day.

Come in for a demonstration daily after 6 in the evening and on Sundays all day.

We sell wholesale and retail. Frig-O-Matic, care of L. Kaufman, 201 Division Avenue, Brooklyn 11, New York."

title: Of Fear and Strangers: A History of Xenophobia
author: George Makari
review: If you are reading a book and come across a paragraph that begins "I went to my shelves and pulled down the Compact Oxford English Dictionary.", you should close the book and congratulate yourself on a few unexpected hours of free time. Because that is a book you do not need to read.

title: Cuba: An American History
author: Ada Ferrer
review:
A good book!

The US has done a lot of harm in Cuba over the years. A lot of it tied to the slave trade
- In 1994 the Monroe doctrine (telling European countries not to mess with the Western hemisphere) kept slavery in Cuba by keeping the UK out.
- In the 1930s a sitting senator illegally operated a business that sold slaves in Cuba
- During the civil war, confederate businessmen shipped slaves to Cuba as an insurance policy in case the North won. And through the late 1800s and early 1900s, as labor conditions improved in the US, businesses turned to Cuba as a place where they could skirt the law and exploit workers
- The US refused to let Cuba be autonomous: they imposed a constitution on Cuba in 1901s. In 1934 the US flat out forced Cuba to change their president, and they did. In 1959 the US protested Cuban agricultural reform in order to protect US landholders

An important piece of economic context to keep in mind with all of this: When you control for whether or not a country gets preferable economic support from democratic countries, there is no positive effect of being democratic on economic development. In other words: Democracy does not make countries rich. But being friendly with big important democracies (like the US) does. So conversely, the US economically harming Cuba has made Cuba poor.

Of course the US is not the only actor causing harm in Cuba. Castro's socialist government socialist government did not allow political opposition or a free press. And: "Cuban communism has solved all but three problems: breakfast, lunch, and dinner."

But it is not all bad! Life expectancy in Cuba is higher than in the US!

title: Mao: The Unknown Story
author: Jung Chang
review:
It's important to fact check history books, and very easy to do so with chatgpt! Originally I had 5 interesting bits from this book, but after checking them it turned out 2 weren't true, and 1 was highly exaggerated.

--

Overall this book was a detailed, readable, but very one-sided account of Mao's life. Not like I'm a fan of Mao, but the book reads like a hit piece rather than an objective account of his life (which would be damning enough). Apparently lots of the claims are highly exaggerated or not-well substantiated.

The most important claims are true: Mao was a extremely adept at navigating pollical currents around him and amassing power. He used this power to create an extremely powerful state, and killed tens of millions of his own citizens. You don't need a 600-page book to tell you that.

Some interesting bits:
1. In the early 40s, the Chinese Communist Party under Mao grew and sold opium as an income source
2. The CCP got a big boost in the late 40s in their war against the nationalists when the US put pressure on the nationalists to seek peace (in particular by halting arms sales to the nationalists). this allowed the CCP to consolidate their position before eventually making a successful campaign and driving the nationalists to Taiwan

title: Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern World
author: Jack Weatherford
review:
A short, readable history of the Mongolian empire.

Gives you a good appreciation for how good of a manager GK was - he was very good at spotting talent. I had not understood the extent to which the Mongols were constantly taking the best workers from the places they conquered, and putting them to work improving their army and their civilization.

If you are a government who wants to provide luxuries for your people, but your society doesn't produce anything that other people want, then the only way to acquire luxuries is to steal them from rich people nearby.

It seems to overstate its case about how admirable the Mongols were, but I understand it's trying to combat overly negative perceptions of Genghis Khan in the west.

title: Long for This World: The Strange Science of Immortality
author: Jonathan Weiner
review: I thought this would be mostly about the science. Turns out it's more about the eons-long-quest for immortality. After being confronted with so many quotes from Egyptian scrolls, Greek wise men, and  Shakespeare, I am less interested in the science.

title: Getting to Yes: Negotiating Agreement Without Giving In
author: Roger Fisher
review:
Very practical:
- be soft on people, hard on the problem
- negotiate over interests, not positions
- explore different potential BATNAs (Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement) thoroughly. It gives you clarity during the negotiation

Could have been a pamphlet.

title: Cro-Magnon: How the Ice Age Gave Birth to the First Modern Humans
author: Brian M. Fagan
review:
What would it be like to be a (anatomically modern) human, walking around on the plains, and to see off in the distance a fundamentally different species of human (neanderthals)? This book has a lot of good vivid speculation on what scenarios like that would have felt like for the people experiencing them.

Apparently we are still very early in our understanding of the distant past: This book came out only 15 years ago, and already the scientific consensus on one of its fundamental claims (that homo sapiens and Neanderthals' never interbreeder) has been thoroughly overturned. Those of us of European descent have ~1-2% neanderthal DNA!

title: Talking to Strangers: What We Should Know About the People We Don't Know
author: Malcolm Gladwell
review:
Not for me. Many interesting anecdotes, but I don't trust Gladwell to draw the right generalizations from them.

If talking to strangers is so hard, why do interviews generally work decently well?

title: Unfabling the East: The Enlightenment's Encounter with Asia
author: Jürgen Osterhammel
review: Encouraging to learn that racial science and western smugness towards other cultures were not embedded in the fibers of the enlightenment. Enlightenment thinkers were very curious about other cultures, trying to learn from everyone they could. The really bad stuff came later.

title: Globalization and its Discontents
author: Joseph E. Stiglitz
review:
Compellingly makes the case that the IMF does not serve the interests of the countries it is supposed to stabilize. Basically because:

The conditions it applies to financing do not help the recipient country - it takes a one-size-fits-all, free market / financial liberalization approach that is not grounded in sound economics. But it presents its prescriptions as settled economic consensus.

These policies benefit American banks. Why would the IMF want to benefit American banks? 2 reasons:
1. There is a revolving door between IMF leadership and top Wall Street firms
2. US banks have huge influence on the US Treasury. The US Treasury has huge influence on the IMF.

Similarly the US exerts its international influence to promote free trade when it supports American exports, but not where it would hurt US industry. The US demands free trade on agricultural products, where it subsidizes production and then exports. But then demands that aluminum producers in the US be protected from cheaper foreign competitors.

The book is not really anti-globalization - it is generally pro international commerce. But it is anti-IMF and to some extent the World Bank.

Good honeymoon reading. But too fluffy - should have been 100 pages!

title: Economic And Social History Of Medieval Europe: The Acclaimed Belgian Historian's Account of Western Europe's Roman to Medieval Era (Harvest Book)
author: Henri Pirenne
review:
A real treat!

One of the most interesting bits: Artisan guilds were meant to protect artisans producing for the local market. Their protection did not extend to producers making for export markets - so the split between labor and capital first came about in export markets

Not long after came the first strikes: In 1245, workers in Douai in France struck. And very quickly, strikes become punishable by death or banishment.

title: The Lean Startup
author: Eric Ries
review:
These ideas have totally permeated the fabric of how people think about startups: Almost every recommendation in here is something that we already do at Kapu, often using the exact same terminology.

It was useful to skim through and read the interesting sections!

Nuggets for me to remember
- a startup is a machine that learns and then builds
- Vanity metrics make you think you're doing things right, but actually are useless because they don't track what is actually important. Plus they tempt you to just look at them and say "yay numbers go up", and assume that it is due to an action you took, when really it might be just random noise
- It's critical to use cohort views, because they make it harder to lie to yourself that "things are getting better"
- Your time to pivot as a company should decrease over time
- Ask 5 "why's" when you have a problem
- "If we do not know who the customer is, we do not know what quality is"

title: The Coming Wave: Technology, Power, and the Twenty-first Century's Greatest Dilemma
author: Mustafa Suleyman
review: A decent summary of how our world is going to be rapidly changed by new technological advancements. If you’re already familiar with discussions of technology-driven existential risks (AI, nuclear weapons, biotechnology) then this book probably won’t do much for you.

title: The Subjection of Women
author: John Stuart Mill
review:
I most enjoyed the parts where Mill points out others' hypocrisy, and gets to the root of their real motivations.

For example: he points out that if your logic for legally barring women from certain jobs is "they are unfit for the job", then you don't need to legally bar them! If the women really aren't good at those jobs, then nobody will hire them anyways. Men aren't worried women will be bad at the jobs - they are just worried that if women are allowed to do these jobs then the status of men will fall in society.

He was right, both morally and factually.

Interesting how back then, there was so little data on anything, that claims about society were just based on historical anecdotes and personal experience.

title: Essentialism: The Disciplined Pursuit of Less
author: Greg McKeown
review:
I have a tendency to try to do a bunch of things that ultimately don't matter - in work and in side-projects. This book helped me see the error of my ways.
- Most things you can spend time on simply do not matter.
- Making tiny progress on a bunch of different initiatives prevents you from making tons of progress on one big initiative.
- You have to continuously and deliberately reinforce the habit of pruning, because unimportant things have a way of creeping into your life
- Focus your time and energy only on whatever is most important to you. It means you won’t do things that are less important, but that is ok.

title: The Man Who Sold the World: David Bowie and the 1970s
author: Peter Doggett
review:
Bowie's early career is so boring, but he basically just continued to try out different things until he hits with Ziggy. That was only possible because he was in the right scene in London in the 60s, and had an incredible sense for how to market himself.

What's even more striking is that after hitting it big, he then continues to try different things out throughout the 70s - but now at an incredibly high level.

I think a lot of it is due to good collaboration. Bowie was a great collaborator. And after he was successful, he got to collaborate with great people (especially Carlos Alomar and Brian Eno).

--

Also apparently Bowie lied in basically every single interview he ever gave, saying basically whatever would get him attention.

title: Nomad Century: How Climate Migration Will Reshape Our World
author: Gaia Vince
review:
Retroactively took down from 3 to 2 stars after doing more research and learning that "Predicting the effects of climate change upon migration is extremely challenging, and all forecasts are currently unreliable" (from this report https://www.cgdev.org/sites/default/files/climate-change-and-migration-omnibus-overview-policymakers-and-development.pdf)

She claims quite confidently that climate change will lead to hundreds of millions if not billions of climate migrants. In reality, it is very hard to see what effects climate change will have on migration. (For example - in some instances climate shocks decrease migration, because people can no longer afford to migrate when their livelihoods are destroyed. Typically it is higher-income people who are more likely to migrate, not lower).

She seems to exaggerate both the magnitude of climate-affected migration, and our certainty about how climate will affect migration.

below is my original review - beware! I should not have been so persuaded by her main point.

--

Persuasive and vivid on the the main point: that enormous levels of migration will be required this century for us to deal with climate change.

Not very persuasive on any concrete solutions to this. She's basically saying "we should basically do everything we can to adapt to climate change and facilitate migration". Which fair enough. But I would preferred a deep dive on some specific, realistic solutions. Instead the second half of the book reads like a technocratic liberal wish list of things at various levels of feasibility. Including:
- UN-issued passports
- nuclear fusion electricity production
- universal healthcare
- rooftop gardens
- using toy libraries to reduce waste

I doubt the book will convince anyone to support any climate-adaptation policy they did not already support.

But on that note: It is an interesting illustration that it is hard to answer the question "how should we deal with climate change?" without also answering the question "what would my ideal society look like?"

title: How Migration Really Works: A Factful Guide to the Most Divisive Issue in Politics
author: Hein de Haas
review:
The book is organized around different commonly misheld views about migration. It's useful to flip through and read the sections that correct misconceptions you have.

The main misconception I had was that climate change will lead to mass migration. It is really not as straightforward as this, and the rhetoric saying that we will see waves of climate migrants seems quite alarmist.

Sometimes he argues too much, seemingly just to argue. Let me not cite examples lest I argue with him for arguing too much.

So take what you read here with a grain of salt - his overall goal is to argue against the idea that there is a migration crisis, and it seems that sometimes he pursues this goal at the expense of being as accurate has he could.

But very useful as a check to find where you might have very incorrect beliefs, that you can then research further.

title: Shrewd Samaritan: Faith, Economics, and the Road to Loving Our Global Neighbor
author: Bruce Wydick
review:
It feels ungrateful to be irritated at Wydick for not pushing far enough towards the importance of impact in making decisions about to help others. He’s definitely trying to push Christians to be more thoughtful in their charity, and overall the book probably does that. But I think he doesn’t push far enough — he is too concerned with the effect that a philanthropic act has on the philanthropist, and not enough on the effect it has on the people the act is intended to help.

Partly this comes from his belief that God does not value good acts primarily in terms of their utilitarian outcomes. But also it comes from a belief on his part that mostly people won’t be that motivated by statistics, and need personal connection in order to do good. I hope he is underestimating the extent to which people can be impersonally selfless. He’s pushing for an incremental expansion of our circle of compassion — I want a more radical increase. But maybe I am too optimistic.

He also raises a good point that Amartya Sen’s framework of development as freedom doesn’t allow us to condemn increases in immoral behavior resulting from economic development (e.g., increased internet access increasing consumption of porn). This raises an interesting tension: Should people working in development be focused on only development outcomes? Or on morality outcomes as well? If you are a government I think the answer is pretty clear — you should be focused on only development and not morality. If you are a religiously-based charity the answer is also clear — morality is important. But what if you are an NGO? Or a company? Or an individual attempting to make the world a better place? The answers here are much less clear.

title: THE BOURGEOIS CATHOLICISM VS CAPITALISM IN 18TH CENTURY FRANCE
author: Bernard Groethuysen

title: War and Peace
author: Leo Tolstoy
review:
A book that has changed how I view the world. Has made very vivid for me:
- The total disconnect between what war actually is (confusion and violence), and narratives we build around it (stories of bravery in battle, military decorations and honors, grand strategies)
- How effective government and historical propaganda is at making us regard as "great" people like Napoleon who ought to be considered fiends
- The inability of most people to make a significant difference in the world
- The unwillingness of those who are comfortable to even try
- The senselessness of most people's opinions, including those of "experts"
- Our inability to explain why historical events happen
- The power of nationalism to motivate - for good or for ill

Also very fun.
- The battle scenes are generally exciting, though some go on too long
- Lots of interesting politics in Russian military
- He makes fun of doctors at every opportunity
- Fun depictions of Russian noble country life

There are things in the book that are very hard to relate to:
- The placement of sweet young girls on a pedestal of goodness and beauty
- Tolstoy's essay-length complaints about the faults of historians of his time
But I think there is still value in these, because it makes me confront the ways in which that time was so different from now.

I was ready to have to slog through it, but it is actually very readable. Prose is easy to read in both the Pevear/Volokhonsky and the free version I found on Planet PDF. The chapters are super short - like 2-4 pages each, so it's easy to chunk. And I found it easier to keep track of the characters than in books like Brothers Karamazov or Les Miserables. It's just that it is long - but you can just think of it like reading a book series.

title: The Mom Test: How to talk to customers & learn if your business is a good idea when everyone is lying to you
author: Rob Fitzpatrick
review: One of the most practical books I've read in a while.

title: Napoleon: A Concise Biography
author: David A. Bell
review:
Concise, clear, entertaining. Gave me a sense for Napoleon, his historical context, what he actually did, why he was important, and (maybe most of all) why he is so famous. One of the first to master of using mass media to shape his image and become a worldwide celebrity.

Perfect as background material for reading War and Peace, which is exactly what I wanted it for.

title: The Nine Lives of Pakistan: Dispatches from a Precarious State
author: Declan Walsh
review: I listened on 3x speed. Can't say I retained much.

title: Boomerang: Travels in the New Third World
author: Michael Lewis
review:
I found this book riveting. Full of flawed characters, and hilarious caricatures of Icelandic culture

Here are some claims about the Icelandic:
- Apparently belief in elves - "hidden people" - is common in Iceland. I cannot find validation for this anywhere else online, but Lewis claims that aluminum company Alcoa wanted to build a factory, but "had to defer to a government expert to scour the enclosed plant site and certify that no elves were on or under it."
- Iceland has only 400,000 people. According to Lewis, this makes everyone feel extremely important, because everyone knows the prime minister, and can just walk into his office.
- Everyone also knows Björk: ' “Yes, I know Björk,” a professor of finance at the University of Iceland says in reply to my question, in a weary tone. “She can’t sing, and I know her mother from childhood, and they were both crazy. That she is so well known outside of Iceland tells me more about the world than it does about Björk.”'
- This importance can then lead to frustration that two of the largest industries - aluminum smelting and fishing - do not confer status or pay commensurate with the importance most Icelandic place upon themselves.
- According to Lewis, this culture (self-importance without a productive outlet) contributed to financial hubris leading to the the 2008-2011 Icelandic financial crisis

Also included are funny caricatures of the Irish, Greek, and German, and a description of Arnold Schwarzenegger's morning bicycle routine

author: Eugene Soltes
review: There but for the grace of God go I.

title: The Namesake
author: Jhumpa Lahiri
review:
My kids will have an immigrant parent. This book made me write out a list of what I hope we can provide to our kids so that they feel at home both in multiple cultures.

Because the main lesson from this book is that as a parent if you just try hard enough and plan hard enough, you can make your kid turn out exactly the way you want.

title: Interpreter of Maladies
author: Jhumpa Lahiri
review: I laughed. I didn't cry but I felt sad. It moved me.

title: Utopia
author: Thomas More
review:
I like how he opens by saying "Henry VIII is of course the greatest and most just king who has ever lived", then spends the first third of the book talking about how all princes and lords care only about enriching themselves and their friends at the expense of their subjects.

"I never said the lords were corrupt! It was only the characters in my book that said that."

title: Chip War: The Fight for the World's Most Critical Technology
author: Chris Miller
review:
Chip supply chains have more choke points than I had previously known - it's not just TSMC and ASML. ASML has hundreds of extremely specialized suppliers across Europe. Developing high-end chips requires using one of three software packages, all three companies of which are located in the US. No country can "go it alone" and and produce the highest-end chips without relying on a global network.

Other notes:
- government support, both domestic and foreign government support, has been critical to development of high value manufacturing of chips in the US, Taiwan, Korea, and Japan. US government and military supported development of not only silicon valley but also the silicon industry in east Asia. And in Japan, Korea, and Taiwan the governments took a strong hand in directing investment towards chip manufacturing. For these companies to thrive, it was not only about being innovative to attract capital - it was about having the connections and being in the right place so that government drives capital towards a you
- One of TI's first big contracts was for the minuteman nuclear missiles
- during cold war, soviet students still came to the US to study advanced tech like semiconductors
- Morris Chang was the only Chinese in his class at Harvard and originally studied Shakespeare before transferring to MIT to study Mech E
- Charles De Gaulle said dismissively of the Japanese prime minister that he seemed "like a semiconductor salesman". Powerful countries underestimated the impact of semiconductors
- the Japanese PM had promised to double people's income within 10 years - he straightforwardly accepted importance of materialism in Japan
- book emphasizes (I think accurately) the importance of the opportunity for engineers and entrepreneurs to get super wealthy in silicon valley - which was not possible in Soviet Union

title: Flash Boys: A Wall Street Revolt
author: Michael Lewis
review: I found the book riveting. Full of flawed characters, and lessons about our inability for regulation to outrun people's creativity in cheating one another.

title: Samsung Rising: The Inside Story of the South Korean Giant That Set Out to Beat Apple and Conquer Tech
author: Geoffrey Cain
review:
Interesting overall history of Samsung, and important context about their involvement in corruption in Korea. But at times reads too much like a hit piece.

Samsung is the second-most-important chip manufacturer in the world, second-biggest smartphone manufacturer, makes tons of consumer brands in houses across the world, and is the largest company in a country that is one of the greatest economic success stories of the past 50 years. How have they been able to do this? After reading this book I can tell you that:
- they had a lot of government support
- their American marketing team did a very good job challenging Apple - seemingly in spite of bad ideas from the head office in Korea

On the negative side of Samsung, the book was very robust:
- they have a very top-down-driven corporate culture that suppresses good ideas
- they have extreme loyalty to the owning family - to the extent that managers will sell their company stock at a loss so that the owning family can maintain control
- they are very cozy with corrupt politicians and routinely make bribes

Frusterating because I know there must be much more to the story here of what has made Samsung so fantastically successful, but I don't know what that is because the book is uninterested in that.

Interesting bit: If Samsung went out of business it would basically take the entire south Korean economy with it. Unemployment would go from 3 to 10 percent. The entire insurance industry would fail, and most banks would become insolvent

title: Big Billion Startup: The Untold Flipkart Story
author: Mihir Dalal
review:
Interesting book for its depiction of the startup ecosystem in India. And also interesting if you work in ecommerce
- having investor trust at a startup is not to be taken for granted
- toxic internal politics can also be a huge albatross. Avoiding that is also not to be taken for granted
- People very much doubted that ecommerce could work in India until it did
- IIT seems to catalyze entrepreneurship in India. Less from what students learn there, and more from just throwing all the smart hardworking people together in one place
- Many entrepreneurs first cut their teeth at big global companies - Amazon, McKinsey

title: Tractor Wars: John Deere, Henry Ford, International Harvester, and the Birth of Modern Agriculture
author: Neil Dahlstrom
review:
Too much "this happened then this happened," Not enough "here are the big ideas you should latch onto about how modern agriculture was born."

But fun to read globally important history set in the place that I grew up. And apparently tractor competitions (i.e., agricultural exhibitions) were very important in the early 1900s.

title: My Life And Work (The Autobiography Of Henry Ford)
author: Henry Ford
review:
fun! Morals: Ignore the things that aren’t relevant to your business. As he says, most men cannot deal with more than one problem at a time. And the important thing is not just building the machine - it's building the machine that builds the machine

- Henry doesn’t like wide variety of products, sophisticated pricing, focusing on competitors, speculation on future prices of materials. The moral is not that these things are never good for business (even though he claims they are never good). The moral is that as a business you need to focus on what is most important, and ignore things that aren’t
- For Ford, there was a huge unmet demand for cars that were affordable and reliable. He realized that the core thing Ford could offer was a affordable reliable car. So everything is focused on that. Fancy pricing is a distraction. Variety of products is a distraction. For other businesses those might be important. They were not for Ford, and so he ignored them

title: The Telling
author: Ursula K. Le Guin
review: An excellent entry in the Le Guin franchise of "outsider travels to a planet where the people are vaguely daoist, and learns something"

title: Middlemarch
author: George Eliot
review:
An excellent book to read when you are deciding whether or not to get married. Lots of different types of relationships, explored with lots of nuance. Several time this sparked in me "Ah, I should talk with Jia about how we would handle this type of situation"

Lots of funny snide commentary from the narrator. Lots of people trying to do good but running into conflicts of interest. So very relatable.

Any book about the lives of ordinary people set before 1950 always leaves me with 3 main takeaways:
- Overall life was so hard back then (especially for women)
- I am very grateful to live in an individualistic culture where I don't have strong family/societal expectations about what is proper / improper for me to do
- I am very glad to live in culture where high value is put on clear, honest communication. So many problems come from people not just telling each other how they feel and what they want

There are a lot of parallel's between 1800s England and Confucian China as depicted by Eileen Chang. The importance of family expectations. The place of women. Strong norms about what is proper vs not.

This is now my favorite novel written before 1900.

title: City of Illusions
author: Ursula K. Le Guin
review:
Owns so much. An epic-fantasy style story - mysterious man sets out on a quest to discover his destiny - but set in a sci-fi world. Made me feel like a kid, and made me think.

No author captures the enormity of culture and the vastness of time the way Le Guin does.

title: The Age of Reform (Awarded the Pulitzer Prize for History, 1956): From Bryan to F.D.R.
author: Richard Hofstadter
review:
Lots of interesting things on American history from 1890-1920 in here!

- Early America has romanticizes the non commercial farmer. The "agrarian myth" - indulged by people like Thomas Jefferson - is that there is this yeoman farmer who is individualistic, honest, healthy, and happy. he has integrity, and goodwill towards his fellow man. This is mostly a made-up ideal but it is a core component of America's sense of self.
- This ideal is related to the importance of "property rights"-the farmer can make the best of what he has because he owns it himself
- This idea came into clash with industrialization, and the building of the modern city. People from the countryside would move into the city, but they would retain nostalgia for the country. And some people in the country despised city people with all their immorality and drunkenness and immigrants
- As cities industrialized and commercialized, so too did farms. Farmers needed equipment to farm efficiently. This means they needed financing.
- Rural populism gained popularity in the 90s - driven largely by global recession. Nothing is ever just local in modern history! Global events matter.
- a lot of progressives in ~1900-1925 were anti immigration. They saw immigrants as hurting labor unions, as being easily bought by political machines, and as not conforming quickly enough to American society to be good progressive citizens. They were also drunken Catholics, or greedy Jews, and were hurting the moral fiber of the country. The Johnson-Reed immigration restriction act of 1924, and the 18th amendment banning alcohol both come out of progressivism.
- Progressivism was not born out of deprivation - during the early 1900s, the most people were actually gaining in terms of income - rising tide was raising all boats. But the middle class were losing out to the new business elites in terms of status. This lead to people turning to progressivism.

Aside:
During ww2 farmers were able to get legislation that said if market prices for farm goods rose above the consumer price ceiling, government would make up the difference. To roosevelets chagrin. Shows the power of farm lobby

title: Going Infinite: The Rise and Fall of a New Tycoon
author: Michael Lewis
review:
If someone sounds smart, confident, and rational, we have a tendency to defer to them - to trust them and think they're right, regardless of what they're actually saying.

Listening to the things Sam Bankman-Fried said before the FTX blowup is a very good way to help rid yourself of this unjustified deference.

title: Elon Musk
author: Walter Isaacson
review:
The audiobook is 20 hours long but still feels like it's flying over events and only giving you a very high level picture of Musk. I realized in listening to it that basically ALL biographies are pretty shallow - it's very hard to summarize a person's entire life. I understand now how Robert Caro can be writing a 5 volume biography of LBJ.

Fascinating just how un-strategic and impulsive Musk is. He seems to have a psychological need for stress, and a lot of his cruel treatment of employees and general chaos-mongering seems to be his way to satisfy his emotions. And he just disregards how it makes other people feel. I think we're very lucky that more often than not, his ambition has been aimed at things that are good for humanity.

I'd say the book is 10/10 on readability and interest, 5/10 on insight. And definitely paints a very positive picture of Musk, but I think that's fine as long as you realize the book has this bias.

Of course Musk's greatest crime of his many is distracting Grimes and drastically slowing down the rate which she makes music.

title: The Arc of a Covenant: The United States, Israel, and the Fate of the Jewish People
author: Walter Russell Mead
review:
Great book, not only on the US-Israel relationship, but maybe the best book I've ever read on American politics. Definitely the best book I've read on overall American foreign policy.

Some favorite quotes:
- “Washington’s ability to force smaller and weaker countries to take steps against the wishes of their leaders is much less extensive than most Americans appreciate.”
- “Many people — Jews, antisemites, and others — share a tendency to think that Jews play a larger role in human society than they actually do.”
- “This ‘historicization of the eschaton,” the transfer of speculation about the end of history and/ or the end of the world from the realm of theology and myth to the realm of practical politics, is one of the greatest differences between human culture and self-awareness in our times and in the premodern era.”

Some interesting bits:
- In medeival Europe, common people could not read the bible. Only elites could, so your main exposure to Christian scripture was whatever the church decided to transmit to you. Church ceremonies had a heavy emphasis on Jesus's passion and death - so Christians were constantly being reminded (explicitly or implicitly) that "the jews" killed Jesus
- Around 1560, the Bible started getting mass produced for people to read themselves. People spent a lot of time with the Bible. And 75% of the Bible is the Old Testament - which is Jewish scripture and tells the story of Jewish people. There are all these Jewish heroes, like Abraham, David, Ruth, Solomon, Samson, etc. Tons of Jewish poetry, and law, and fun stories are in the old Testament. So the common people of Europe starting being much much more sympathetic to Jews
- progressives were some of those who put and end to immigration to the US in the 1920s because they worried that immigrants would weaken the labor movement
- The UK economy was so bad after WW2. There was a 6-day period in 1947 when it was SO COLD in the UK that the cabinet decided to pull out of India and Israel and stop supporting Greece nationalism
- Some of the first aspects of common American interest in the welfare of people in other countries came up around Greek independence. Then similar for Italian independence. Jewish restorationism among American Christians grew out of this tradition. Greek, Latin, and Jewish civilization were all ancient civilizations that Americans were familiar with and had warmth towards
- Eleanor Roosevelt was super powerful after FDR had died, and was one of the main forces that pulled Truman's policy - especially foreign policy - to the left
- American foreign policy experts don’t realize how much their promotion of democracy, freedom, etc. are challenges to governments like China, Russia, Iran. And then when what seems like promotion of self-obvious goods from the US is met by violence by Russian and China, and the US has the audacity to be annoyed
- Trump used Israel as a foreign policy issue to unite his base of people who want strong US power abroad and those who want US to not intervene much
- Nationalism manifests itself quite differently in the US vs in Europe. The idea of the melting pot in US makes way more sense when you consider that in in the 1800s all the Poles, Czechs, Irish, Italians, Greeks, French, etc. were all for the first time in a big way buying into the idea that each of them were ethnic nations that should have their own countries. But in the US all these people were living in the same nation - and that nation fashioned its own nationalism partly out of being welcoming to all these people
- Israel policy became much more part of the American right’s agenda from Reagan, who stressed the promotion of democracy abroad, and was supported by evangelicals for whom the restoration of Israel has eschatological importance

Also I bought on both kindle and audible. Ideally this lets you seamlessly go back and forth between reading and listening. When it worked I found this experience quite nice, but it was very very buggy. Would not really recommend unless you really want to both listen and be able to double check things by reading - OR you have a lot of disposable income to be able to buy books twice without worrying about it.

title: Voices from the Chinese Century: Public Intellectual Debate from Contemporary China
author: Timothy Cheek
review:
I read while in China and was helpful to get a bunch of intellectual viewpoints on things I was seeing while traveling, and that I had learned while reading history about China.

Some of my conclusions:
- I think the CCP does not have a strong ideology other than "we want to stay in power"
- the restricting on debate makes it very hard to form coherent ideology
- Chinese people on the whole are pretty happy with their government
- authoritarian regimes use arguments like "the poeple aren't ready yet for democracy" or "if we had democracy it would impede our economic growth". these arguments may or may not be true, but authoritarians will say them REGARDLESS of whether or not they are true.

title: The Cold War's Killing Fields: Rethinking the Long Peace
author: Paul Thomas Chamberlin
review:
Lots of killing, zero-sum mentality and totalizing world views are bad.

I appreciate how he puts the rise of revolutionary Islam in the context of the Cold War - as a reaction against both communism and capitalism.

He also clearly shows the lack of unity amongst communist forces - the China-USSR split, Cambodia and Vietnam fighting. It's easy to say in hindsight but US policymakers seem just very mistaken in thinking that if any country went communist it would automatically position itself unconditionally with the USSR against the US.

title: Israel: A Concise History of a Nation Reborn
author: Daniel Gordis
review:
As described, comprehensive and accessible. Told with a very heavy-handed pro-Israel slant. I appreciated this because if it was not so heavy-handed I probably would not have noticed, not being very familiar with the history.

I especially valued the context on Theodor Herzl, the importance of poetry in Israel's reckoning with history and the present, and the factors (besides the obvious) that lead to Israelis to feel like their back is up against the wall.

title: The Doomsday Machine: Confessions of a Nuclear War Planner
author: Daniel Ellsberg
review: More good context on why nuclear war is possible, and still bad. And why all out nuclear war is VERY bad.

title: The Bomb: Presidents, Generals, and the Secret History of Nuclear War
author: Fred Kaplan
review:
I never really understood the military industrial complex until reading this book.

Much of the nuclear arms build-up by the US was driven by competition between branches of the armed forces. the Air Force became independent after WW2, and wanted to be the most relevant and most powerful branch of the military. Best way to do that was to have bombs.

The war plan of the US during the cold war was to wipe dozens of cities off the map. Killing hundreds of millions of civilians in both the USSR and China - EVEN IF THE US WASN'T AT WAR WITH CHINA. It was assumed that if we fought the USSR, China would be involved, so the only maneuvers planned for were those that attacked both countries.

The Strategic Air Command was able to create military plans with incredibly little oversight from the president. Eisenhower, Kennedy, Nixon, Carter all tried to get more sensible plans in place, but they weren't able to because of the political power of the military. The military would hide the full extent of the war plan from the presidents so that they would be left alone.

My favorite anecdote was when Kennedy wanted to read the US's nuclear war plan, the Air Force wouldn't let him. Someone - the secretary of State or something - requested to some officer for the report to be shared and they had an exchange like this:

Secretary: Please share the nuclear war plan. The president would like to read it
officer: I can't do that
Secretary: I think you didn't understand. The PRESIDENT is personally requesting the war plan
Officer: Maybe we can have a meeting to brief him on it
Secretary: He would prefer to read it. He is a very good reader
Officer: I will have to check with my boss

In the end Kennedy was not given the war plan, and was instead given a briefing where the officers could massage the messaging to obfuscate how insane the war plan was.

Thank goodness the cold war is over now and nobody has to worry about nuclear weapons ever again

title: The Cold War: A World History
author: Odd Arne Westad
review:
I could not have asked for a better book to get an overall overview of the Cold War. I'm going to write a blog post in more detail but my main takeaways are:
- The biggest lesson is that a zero-sum us vs. them mentality is wrong - both morally and as a framework for making prudent decisions
- The description of US and China as being in a Cold War now is not a good analysis
- I understand how in the aftermath of World War II - having just defeated the ludicrously evil force of Nazi Germany under Hitler - it was easy for Americans and Europeans to believe that the USSR under Stalin was an incredibly evil force that had to be defeated at almost any cost. Understandable sentiment, but this shallow analysis of the situation had very costly repercussions

Also, in the 70s China invaded Vietnam. In the 4 week war, the Chinese lost half as many soldiers (25k) as the US lost in a decade of the Vietnam war (50k). I had never even heard of this invasion until reading this book. Pretty crazy.

title: Korea: The Impossible Country
author: Daniel Tudor
review:
I'm on a Cold War kick, thought this was more of a history book rather than a general interest look at Korean culture. So I skimmed for the parts most interesting to me. I didn't retain very much so honestly a big L for me overall. Not the book's fault though and at least it was free on Audible.

According to the author there is a very important notion of relationship between people - a type of friendship that includes a sense of duty. Depending on the context it can be used for friends, people in the same city, or the entire country. I can't remember the name for it and I can't remember very much about it but it seems very important in Korea.

title: The Cultural Revolution: A People's History, 1962-1976
author: Frank Dikötter
review:
Very good overview. A bit too detailed at times for me. Author seems to have a Libertarian bias (not overwhelmingly, just to be aware of).

My main takeaway is how non-idealogical Mao was. In the sense that, during the cultural revolution, any view that is lauded by the party today might tomorrow be seen as Capital-roader revisionism and get you exiled. The only way to be sure that you would remain in favor next month was to just continuously praise Mao.

It's astounding that he was able to maintain this level of control - but he was a master of managing the changing tides to weaken his rivals while staying in power. In 50s he said the people should air their grievances - their criticism weakened his opponents. And then when people spoke out too much he clamped down on dissent in such a manner that the remaining powerful party members fell in line with him against the "radicals" in society. When the CCP made huge blunders, he would offer a token apology and then get other party members to admit full fault.

A key outcome of the Cultural Revolution was hollowing out of the power that low-ranking party members had. This allowed people in the countryside to start quietly (illegally) privatizing small-scale farms - crossing the river by feeling for the stones. Deng Xiaoping leveraged and institutionalized this once it proved successful, and it kickstarted China's growth from the 70s onwards.

I finish the book with a stronger belief in the importance of free expression of ideas. If you give anyone the ability to limit the expression of ideas, then the state can use that limitation to opress people.

Some other interesting facts
⁃ The CCP made radios cheaper so the entire country could more easily be taught Mao Zedong thought. Ironically had the effect of letting people hear foreign broadcasts spreading capitalist drivel
- I was surprised to learn that Mao was not bloodthirsty in the way Stalin was. I had assumed that Mao was always killing his subordinates - this was not the case. Shows my bias.
⁃ After CR leaders set term limits and prevented power from being consolidated in any one person in the same way that it had been in Mao. The CCP acknowledged the CR was bad but was basically like “don’t talk about it too much. We don’t want you trying to have your own view of history”

title: Laozi's Dao De Jing
author: Lao Tzu
review:
I had tried to read the Dao De Jing before and found it hard to understand and not super compelling. I love the way Ken Liu approaches it - mixing in personal reflections, stories from Zhuangzi, and historical context. I found it a very calming listen.

I also feel I give to much authority to classics like this while I am listening to them. I had this recurrent phenomena of hearing something in the book, and thinking "wait I don't think I agree with that. What is wrong with me disagreeing with the sage master Lao Zi? Wait - I am Catholic, not Daoist so it makes since that I don't agree with everything."

title: The Strangest Man: The Hidden Life of Paul Dirac, Mystic of the Atom
author: Graham Farmelo
review: https://www.modelsandmorality.com/blog/beauty-in-physics-and-paul-dirac

title: Factory Girls: From Village to City in a Changing China
author: Leslie T. Chang
review:
Vivid picture of what life is like for the girls who work in factories in Dongguan. If you are reading this and you think you work hard, you probably don't work as hard as the girls depicted in this book.

Makes me feel very lucky for my life.

Some claims in the book that I found interesting:
⁃ Men are tied to the countryside much more than women - they have a home there given to them by their parents. The women are more likely to leave and make life elsewhere
- In Dongguan, migrants from the countryside don’t worry about discrimination from locals because they almost never meet locals
- These factory workers live very much in the moment, jumping from job to job, from phone to phone, unable to and uninterested in planning very far ahead

title: Niels Bohr and the Infinitely Small
author: Jacques G. Richardson
review:
A good collection on the impact of Neils Bohr as a leader of the physics community as quantum mechanics was being developed, as well as a voice for openness between nations in the face of potential nuclear war after World War II.

Bohr was incremental in his theoretical approach instead of searching for a grand theory. As opposed to Einstein who was troubled by the overarching theoretical implications of quantum mechanics, Bohr took a more practical approach. “It’s paradoxical, but it works”. Science has followed Bohr on this much more than Einstein - taking the "shut up and calculate" of the Copenhagen interpretation.

Instead of searching for a unifying theory, Bohr had this idea of “complementarity”. It means “you can talk about the same subject in two very different kinds of terms, and that what makes good sense in one context can make absolutely no sense in another”. Bing AI summarizes: Therefore, there is no “single picture” that unifies the results obtained in different experimental contexts, and only the “totality of the phenomena” together can provide a completely informative description.

Quantum mechanics was developed at Bohr's institute in Copenhagen in a spirit of great international collaboration. Bohr saw that the nuclear bomb fundamentally changes how countries need to look at national security. In conversations with world leaders (and in a letter to the UN included in this collection) he emphasized that distrust between nations leads to a distorted understanding of of facts and motives. These distortions will lead us to destroy ourselves. We instead need a renewed sense of openness and collaboration between nations.

title: The Lost Metal (Mistborn, #7)
author: Brandon Sanderson
review:
Brandon just sets it up and knocks it down.

Of course he has created my favorite fantasy universe out there, and I love learning more about the mythology, and seeing more and more cross over between characters from different worlds.

But the more I read his books the more I appreciate his strong sense of morality. I'm always surprised and impressed iwth the nuance in the lessons his characters learn, and the unexpected places their arcs land in. It teaches me about character without being overly didactic. I think he is a very wise person.

I am so excited to keep living in the cosmere well into my middle age.

title: Half a Lifelong Romance
author: Eileen Chang
review: One of the most infuriating books (in the sense of inducing righteous fury) that I have ever read.

title: Love in a Fallen City
author: Eileen Chang
review:
My biggest takeaway is the tragedy of being trapped in societal and family expectations that highly limit your ability to be happy - especially for women in 30s China but this phenomenon exists more generally.

My favorites were "Aloeswood Incense: The First Brazier" and "Red Rose White Rose"

I found "Aloeswood Incense" quite affirming of my belief that it can be very harmful to overly value material things and money.


The class unfairness is really aggravating - when the servants play the same games as the mistresses, they get beaten. They live so helplessly in the power of their employers. But I feel that in the end the servant who gets sent away to the countryside probably has the happiest outcome - even if she doesn't see it that way.

These stories make me appreciate how much I take for granted my own freedom and ability to be carefree - I'll be able to land on my feet whatever happens. I have more understanding for people who place high value on optionality and security.

title: Lust, Caution and Other Stories
author: Eileen Chang
review:
Title story and Great Felicity were great - the rest of them I could take or leave.

I read the Lust Caution after watching the movie. It's always fun - for good movies based on good books - to see how the medium of film vs. written word leads to different emphases in the story. In the story we get to see into Jiazhi's heart, that she only feels purpose when she's with Yi, and that this feeling of purpose is transformed into compassion for him. In the movie she is much more unknowable - you don't have a clear understanding about why she decides to warn Yi at the end.

Great Felicity just really makes me feel for women who are trapped in a social situation where they have to put up with bad (from my perspective) marriages.

title: The Horse, the Wheel, and Language: How Bronze-Age Riders from the Eurasian Steppes Shaped the Modern World
author: David W. Anthony

title: Mao's Great Famine: The History of China's Most Devastating Catastrophe, 1958-62
author: Frank Dikötter
review:
A very persuasive history of the factors that lead to the famine:
- top-down commands (e.g., about how to plant seeds) that went against the practical knowledge that farmers had
- export targets that were met at the expense of local consumption in order to show the world how much they were producing
- incentives up and down the government against truth-telling (e.g., to lie about production, to say things were going well when they weren't)
- extraordinary violence used against shirkers

More detail at parts than I really needed.

Before reading I also assumed Mao was more like Stalin in terms of executing and jailing political opponents. He seems really not to have done this much or at all.

Something to note that I learned after reading this book: Since 1947, India has had more malnutrition deaths than China, even including the Great Famine in China. So the Great Famine is an important piece of what can happen under authoritarian power like the CCP, but you have to balance that view with the overwhelming success China has had since 1979.

title: City of Gold: Dubai and the Dream of Capitalism
author: Jim Krane
review:
A good book to skim if you are traveling to Dubai which I was. I'd recommend the first few chapters for historical context and also the chapters on citizenship and sex workers in Dubai.

I learned the UAE has the highest per-capita energy consumption in the world - and during the summer 90% of electricity is spent on air conditioning.

title: Running the Light
author: Sam Tallent
review: Before reading this book I thought it might be kind of cool to get addicted to alcohol and cocaine, but after reading it I'm not so sure.

title: To Live by Hua Yu (2013-08-26)
author: Yu Hua
review: I cried and I've never cried at a book before. One of the most empathy-inducing books I've ever read.

title: Age of Ambition: Chasing Fortune, Truth, and Faith in the New China
author: Evan Osnos
review:
Was recommended to read by my Chinese girlfriend to understand China better before visiting. Gives a good overview of a lot of the different forces affecting Chinese society.

Especially interesting to me:
- The continuous dance between the press and the propoganda department, the press feeling out what will be ok to publish on and what will not be ok
- the fact that lots of Chinese protest and anger is focused on corruption rather than against what the west wishes it was about (e.g., authoritarianism, freedom of speech)
- The Chinese love of numerically categorizing concepts. e.g., the four noes and one without, the three represents, the three supremes
- Grass mud horses and river crabs

title: The Right to Sex: Feminism in the Twenty-First Century
author: Amia Srinivasan
review:
Super thought-provoking and also a page-turner.

Some thoughts I arrived at
- Powerful institutions have the potential to use the power given given in repressive ways - Even when given power ostensibly in the case of fighting oppression (e.g., stricter sexual assault rules at Colgate college seem to have lead to more black students being falsely accused of sexual assault).
- It seems that she has an implicit assumption that that sexual relations in society should be expected to majorly involve sex outside of marriage. It seems unreasonable to expect that a large portion of society switches to having only marital sex. But is it more unreasonable than expecting the overthrow of political influence on who we desire? Or the elimination of systemic sexism and racism? If more people were committed only to have sex in mutually loving relationships with lifelong partners, it would solve a lot of problems in how people approach sex
- Similarly when she discusses porn, she doesn't really question whether in general porn is ok or not. I guess she thinks it's a moot point that people will watch porn and so we need to focus on removing the function of porn as training people to perform (and receive) sexual violence
