- I think she doesn't go far enough when talking about how we should try to shape our own desires. She says that we ought to discipline not "desire itself but the political forces that presume to instruct it." If we were freed from political pressure telling us who is fit to desire (e.g., light-skinned skinny people) we might still be left with evolutionary desires that are distasteful (e.g., desire pretty people). We still have moral obligation to regulate our evolutionary urges (similar to how we don't resort to physical violence as often as we might naturally be inclined). But I agree that the bigger battle now is politics
- And I find myself thinking about and noticing "patriarchy" in the sense of "the implicit training we all receive to see women and sex in harmful ways"

--

There is a tension that arises on the left:
- When your primary value is "dismantle prevailing power structures"...
- ...and you focus on the political content of people's personal choices...

..then it's hard to find people to work and collaborate with. Every person living in society is making some choices - if only by complacency - that uphold part of the system that you want to take down. So you are always compromising with people who are supporting the evil in society.

I think this is not such an issue in liberalism where it is easier to isolate and focus on particular issues.

So I like her point that we should not look to political activism as a safe space. Activism is where you make compromise and get things done. You have to find your safe space and home elsewhere

title: China's Second Continent: How a Million Migrants Are Building a New Empire in Africa
author: Howard W. French
review: Interesting overview of how a bunch of different Chinese in Africa view their home.

title: Aristotle's Children: How Christians, Muslims, and Jews Rediscovered Ancient Wisdom and Illuminated the Middle Ages
author: Richard E. Rubenstein
review: I hadn't realized how different Aristotle and Plato were, or what a revelation Aristotle was to medieval thinkers. Helpful to understand how much of my thought is influenced by Aristotle, and how Christianity is a fusion of both Aristotle's love of nature, logic, and reason, and Plato's love of forms

title: The Silk Road: A New History
author: Valerie Hansen
review: Very good (as far as I know) for giving a sense of what life and economic activity were like in central asia between ~200-1000. Buddhism dominant, no large caravans, extremely multicultural, most trade was local trade or official government business (especially from the Tang empire). Also gives a good sense for how archaeology happens - lucky finds of small scraps of paper, Europeans lying to local people about their intentions, excavating in harsh conditions under time pressure.

title: Turkey: What Everyone Needs to Know®
author: Andrew Finkel
review:
Nice, concise, readable overview of what Turkey is like especially politically.

~10% of the population lives on less than $5 / day
Interesting overview of Turkey's relationship with Europe, EU membership, occupation of Northern Cyprus
Helped me understand why Turks don't like portraying what happened to Armenians in WW1 as a "genocide"

title: Osman's Dream: The History of the Ottoman Empire
author: Caroline Finkel
review: Skimmed. A good reference book on the Ottoman empire. A bit dry to read straight through in my view.

title: The Ottoman Empire, a Great Courses audio book from audible
author: Kenneth W. Harl
review: Good general history. I would have appreciated more on day to day life and less on battles, but no major complaints.

title: The Ottoman Age of Exploration
author: Giancarlo Casale
review: Convinced me that we should think of the Ottomans as having a maritime empire in the same way that the Portuguese did - and competed with the Portuguese. Interesting to me was how protecting the Muslim world - especially enabling the Haj, was a justification for much of what the Ottomans did

title: Planet of Exile
author: Ursula K. Le Guin
review: Deep personal connection in the context of fear/uncertainty of the alien seems to be something Le Guin explores a lot and is really good at. I love the contrast of the nomadic with the settled people in this book too.

title: Rocannon’s World
author: Ursula K. Le Guin
review: There's a nobility and traditionalism in the aliens and in the prose style of the book that I find bittersweet when contrasted with the high tech of the Hainish. It's like they are holding on to their way of life in the face of this crushing tide of scientific advancement, and as the reader I just have this sense that it won't end well for them.

title: The Silk Roads: A New History of the World
author: Peter Frankopan
review: Did not finish the last third of the book. This is not a book on the silk road - it is a history of the entire world book with a relatively large focus on Central Asia. Given that, it's pretty good.

title: Crossroads: A Popular History of Malaysia and Singapore
author: Jim Baker
review: Skimmed it because I was planning to travel to Malaysia and Singapore (didn't end up happening). Good as a general history of Malaysia and Singapore - the long history of the Malay people, the strong influence from Indian subcontinent on societal structure, the importance of the Malaka Straight in shipping, and then the creation of Singapore as a separate state. Recommended to anyone traveling there.

title: The Lathe of Heaven
author: Ursula K. Le Guin
review: Great concept, love the way the concept is built out and explored. I love the conflict in the scientist character - wanting to make the world better and believing that he is wise enough to get rid of all evils if he just had enough power. The opening paragraph is so beautiful.

title: Beautiful World, Where Are You
author: Sally Rooney
review:
I had seen Sally Rooney show up on my friends' Goodreads and heard her described as a great millennial writer. I did not expect this to be one of the top 3 "most Catholic books" I've ever read.

People have a tendency to be bad. The world can seem very grim. We try to find meaning in the world - something that transcends everyday existence.

Without an a set of organizing principles for their lives (such as the structure of religion), the characters struggle to understand how to live. Can it be as simple as loving the people around you? Finding meaning in work? Can people truly be redeemed when they can be so bad? Am I lovable?

The book is not saying "you have to be religious to get satisfactory answers to these questions." But I do feel like it is saying "the rejection of religion leaves a gap - and you have to answer these questions somehow"

I also feel like the book is very traditional somehow. It's not subtle. 1/3 of the book is emails between two characters where they share exactly what they think (or pretend to at least).

title: Lolita
author: Vladimir Nabokov
review:
I'm glad I read it. Not a fun book.

Feels like it is supposed to be very much about America somehow, but in a way that for me is unresolved and doesn't really click.

Best parts to me is how HH spends pages and pages talking about how he feels about Lolita, only for then to be some small description of something she actually does that makes you realize you don't know her as a character at all.

title: Trick Mirror: Reflections on Self-Delusion
author: Jia Tolentino
review: Super thought-provoking, entertaining, challenging, readable. She has such good insights about how it feels for people in my social class in the US, especially on the internet. I don't mood affiliate with her on capitalism - she likes to in the middle of an exploration of a bad thing say "of course capitalism is the root of these problems and can't be sustained" - but it's relatively easy to ignore these statements.

title: Conquerors: How Portugal Forged the First Global Empire
author: Roger Crowley
review:
A decent overview of how the Portuguese global trading empire started, with lots of focus on key military battles in India from 1500-1515. I had hoped it would cover a broader time period, and focus more on the Malaysia area and the decline of the Portuguese empire, but it's good for what it is.

Gets across the idea that the Portuguese learned FAST. In around 5 years they go from landing in India for the first time and confusing Hindus for a deviant sect of Christianity, to understanding the politics enough to work Indian princes against each other and develop a stranglehold on the region.

Before Bartolemu Diaz sailed around Africa in 1488, Europeans thought that Africa might extend all the way to the south pole an be impossible to go around. I understand now what a big deal it was to be able to travel by sea to the Indian ocean.

Also apparently the Portuguese discovered Brazil by accident when sailing to India. And people really didn't understand scurvy at all until the 1800s. 1/3 of Portugeuese sailors died between 1500-1515.

title: Merchant Kings: When Companies Ruled the World, 1600 - 1900
author: Stephen R. Bown
review:
Fascinating, makes me want to learn so much more about this time period and about all these trading companies.

The scope of ambition that some of these men had, and their ruthlessness in pursuing it is astounding. The fact that many of them thought they were morally in the right (when I look back and see them committing so many obvious atrocities) makes me feel much more humble about my ability to know that what I am doing is right and will stand up to the test of history.

I had not really understood the extent of Dutch influence in North America (New Netherland/New Amsterdam). Or really their influence on the world overall. The Dutch East Indies company made up 50% of European foreign trade in 1650!

title: One Mighty and Irresistible Tide: The Epic Struggle Over American Immigration, 1924-1965
author: Jia Lynn Yang
review:
Very good for foundation and historical background on how imimgration to the US has worked. The 1965 immigration bill is still the framework used for US immigration.

The reason family-based immigration is such a key part of US immigration is because in the ~1920-1960s, WASP Americans didn’t want inferior types like Southern Europeans (Catholic) or Eastern European (Jewish) entering (not to mention Asians/Africans/Hispanics). By accepting mostly people who already had family in the US, they hoped that it would mean more people who were - like the majority of Americans at the time, WASPs.

JFK consciously decided to position himself as an Irish-American (something that hadn't been a core part of his identity before) in order to win political points with immigrants/families of immigrants.

I hadn't realized how restricted overseas immigration was between 1924-1965. However, there was basically an open border with Mexico during this whole time.

This taught me so much about the unexpected consequences laws have. Family-based immigration is now used a lot by groups who are not a large part of the US population. Western Hemisphere caps on immigration were put in place before there was even much immigration from e.g., Mexico. People really did not expect many people to want to immigrate from Asia.

There's a shift in how politicians talk about undesirable immigrants from the 20s-50s: It goes from eugenics-based talk about genetic fitness to talk about undesirable cultural background.

title: The Orphans of Davenport: Eugenics, the Great Depression, and the War over Children's Intelligence
author: Marilyn Brookwood
review:
This book is probably more pro-Iowa than any other book I have read is pro any state. I'm from Davenport and have a brother with Down Syndrome, so there's definitely wishful thinking on my part to believe that historically Iowa has been at the front of anti-eugenics and nurturing children who would otherwise be left behind. But from what I can tell based on what is presented in this book, there is some truth to this view.

Basically, in the 1930s, Psychologists thought that IQ was fixed by genetics, that environment didn't matter that much, and that maybe people with low IQs should be sterilized. Biologists had largely dropped these views, but they persisted in psychology.

Then some researchers at University of Iowa realized:
- hmm, when we put kids from intelligent parents in orphanages where they are neglected, they get less intelligent
- hey, when kids who don't seem smart are taken from neglectful orphanages and put with loving families, they get smarter
- wow, the longer a kid is exposed to neglect, the less intelligent they seem to be

These were wild and surprising findings at the time and caused an uproar in the US psychology community. They were essentially buried, the researchers reputations' tarnished, and everyone went back to thinking that genetics were all that mattered. Then the Nazis made that super unfashionable, and psychology finally moved away from eugenics post WW2.

A very interesting book if you're interesting in the history of psychology, Iowa, or attitudes towards intelligence/eugenics. I skim-read the book in ~2 hours. It's nice that someone cataloged all this detail about the personalities involved, but it wasn't what I was interested in.

Other interesting bits:
- Basically none of rural Iowa had no electricity in the 30s (tracks with what my grandma has told me)
- babies in the Davenport home (now Annie Wittenmeyer for any Davenportians) were basically just put in cribs and left to sit there for months. They were fed and changed, but the only stimulation they had was the sunlight on the ceiling: "Light to shadows to darkness and then light again would have been everything she learned about the world."
- The culture of the Iowa Station (research station at University of Iowa) was critical to allowing the truth-seeking - rather an accepting given psychological dogma. Great management and institutions really matter!

xposted from my blog: www.modelsandmorality.com/blog/anti-eugenics-research-in-1930s-iowa

title: Uncle Vanya
author: Anton Chekhov
review:
Read it mostly because the scenes of it in Drive My Car were so good. It is so good!

The idea of trying not to be dragged down by the apathy of your culture felt very relevant. Feels cliche - great works always feel relevant right? That's why they are classics.

title: Indian Sun: The Life and Music of Ravi Shankar
author: Oliver Craske
review:
I hadn't realized the extent to which so much of the music I love was influenced by Ravi Shankar. Obviously the Beatles, but also Phillip Glass and the other minimalists, and John Coltrane (named his son Ravi!) Drones, a higher focus on rhythm, and re-centering the position of classical composers as also being performers all came from Indian classical music, and Indian classical music came to the west via Shankar.

I'm so glad to live in a time AFTER Ravi Shankar, where we take for granted having access to music from all over the world. It just makes me think music was so constrained sonically before the 60s - all the Beatles had to do was add a sitar to "Norwegian Wood" to be considered revolutionaries. Now pop music has so many different sounds that very little is weird.

I was also struck by:
- being a transcultural performer is so much about personality and ability to package your culture approachably
- having a high profile spurs creativity - Shankar was always having new musical ideas, up until he died. This is much easier when all the best musicians in the world want to collaborate you and share ideas - they give you ideas. A virtuous cycle
- the tension between him and the hippies is funny - he appreciates their support, but also continuously tells them not to smoke and drink at his concerts, and to stop associating his music with tripping
- I did not know he was raped as a child

Nora Jones is the daughter of Ravi Shankar - this will never cease to be one of my favorite music fun facts.

title: Going Down River Road (African Writers)
author: Meja Mwangi
review:
A good empathy machine book on life of a manual laborer in Nairobi in the 70s. One scene in particular really puts you in the mindset of being resignedly helpless in the face of authoritarianism + little economic opportunity.

Good for learning lots of Kenyan slang too, though it's 70s slang so probably not so relevant anymore.

title: East of Eden
author: John Steinbeck
review:
Every few pages there was a observation or character moment that struck me and made me think. Very cool how characters can feel like archetypes while also being complex enough to seem real, especially Sam Hamilton, Lee, Cal. Cathy is maybe an exception.

One of my favorite parts was how you see history moving along - people start driving cars, we move from the Civil War to the first World War, the author places himself in the story reminding you that this took place long ago - and the internal struggle of good vs. evil takes place against the backdrop of this sweeping forward of history/progress. There's only one story - the times change but the conflict doesn't.

title: The Man Who Knew Infinity: A Life of the Genius Ramanujan
author: Robert Kanigel
review:
Four super interesting pictures in this book:
- A picture of Ramanujan himself, as a superb mathematician, a spiritual person, and likely someone who was quite lonely and out of place
- A picture of life in Southern India under British rule, including family dynamics, the spirituality of Southern India, the strict educational system
- A picture of mathematical life at Cambridge, including the Tripass, homosexuality among students and professors, how many professors lived pure academic bachelor lives, and the lack of focus on formal proof in British math vs. continental math until Hardy came along
- A high-level biography of GH Hardy

Think the book does a pretty good job of giving you an idea of the type of math Ramanujan (and Hardy) did, without getting into too much weeds.

I really like learning about a place and culture via biographies. Going to read a biography of Ravi Shankar next to learn more about northern India.

title: The Selected Poems of Li Po
author: Li Po
review: Listened to audiobook, so didn't reflect on each poem as much as I could have. But nice for making me be in the moment, appreciate small things, and have better perspective on life.

title: Owning the Earth: The Transforming History of Land Ownership
author: Andro Linklater
review:
Seems to be a good overview of what it describes! My main takeaways:
- Realized that the idea of property ownership as an unalienable right is really truly foundational to the foundation of American ideology, based especially in Locke, and that I don't really believe it.
- Understanding that everywhere in the world before the 1700s,having authority over land was not absolute. A lord might get the benefit from the crops, but was in turn expected to care for the workers
- owning land also led people to take more pride in their homes
- extending ideas of land ownership to things like intellectual property have been harmful
- seeing land as capital to be invetsed in, improved, and managed is part of what drives economic growth. People didn't necessarily do this before land was "owned" the way we think of it now

title: Drunk
author: Jackson Biko
review: Gripping, funny, sad, well-written. A great empathy machine and a quick read.

title: The Scout Mindset: Why Some People See Things Clearly and Others Don't
author: Julia Galef
review:
Put off reading it because I thought "ah, well I know a lot about the nonrational errors people make, and strategies to avoid making them." But Galef knows her readers know all those already and are still irrational anyways, and so really focuses this book on being more about inspiring you to WANT to be rational. It worked for me.

Very fun and readable and made having a scout mindset sound super appealing. Because we can't just will ourselves to do things, we need aspirational models and to be convinced that actually there are ways to achieve most of the things ew like about irrationality by being rational (eg you may think you need to justify your own incorrect beliefs as a defense mechanism, but why not just instead take pride in learning something new?)

title: Digital Democracy, Analogue Politics: How the Internet Era is Transforming Politics in Kenya (African Arguments)
author: Nanjala Nyabola

title: Why We Fight: The Roots of War and the Paths to Peace
author: Christopher Blattman
review:
Basically, wars are actually not so common relative to all the times they could break out. Wars are value-destructive and very bad for most people, so most of the time people find compromises without resorting to prolonged organized violence. Five main things that can make bargains less likely:
1. Leaders' incentives not aligned with society's, so they can benefit from fighting even if society doesn't
2. Intangible incentives like national pride or moral principles make bargaining seem weak or unattractive or impossible (or even make fighting seem good)
3. Uncertainty about the strength of the other leads to fighting as a means to determine their strength
4. Misperceptions like overconfidence, groupthink
5. Commitment problems - neither side can credibly commit to a bargain

I found this framework super interesting and useful to help me think about conflict!

title: Liang and Lin: Partners in Exploring China's Architectural Past
author: Wilma Fairbank
review:
Life was so hard then and there! The frequency with which Lin and Liang face debilitating sickness that puts them out of commission for 6+ months, horrendous travel during wartime that puts them off the grid for 6+ months, or bombings that put them away from home for years, it's amazing that they were able to do so much in academic architecture. Made me newly appreciative of medicine and peace.

I didn't really know anything about either of them before reading the book and I still can't totally understand how academic architects could be so famous.

Other interesting things:
- when internally displaced eastern Chinese moved to Yunnan during WW2, they were seen by the locals as invaders basically the same as the Japanese. From what I understand this kind of inter-Chinese animosity is not nearly as strong anymore in Yunnan.
- Liang Chichao talks about how must he abhorred and detested Xu Zhimo's decision to marry, but still officiated and gave a very stern and disapproving speech at the wedding. A very different way of showing disapproval than I would do
- at one point some aunts don't want the author and her husband to visit out of fear that a yet-inconceived baby intended for Liang and Lin might end up with the Americans instead
- Seemingly Lin was instrumental to a lot of the architectural work, but her role was not fore-fronted because nobody would really believe that a woman did that much
- I had never before reading this heard "the bamboo curtain" used to refer to Chinese isolationism under Mao
- very interestiing to hear the American author's views on China in the mid-1900s. Doesn't really seem condescending to me, but there's a kind of "I want the reader to understand that this culture is different" attitude in a way that I feel I don't see that much in modern writing. e.g., saying that while in school, Liang was "Chinese to his core" and loved his father but still became American. Talking about balancing the airs of the old and the new in Chinese culture. And in reference to a traditional woman: "her feet were bound and so was her mind"

title: When We Cease to Understand the World
author: Benjamín Labatut
review:
For me the actual theories of quantum mechanics are more beautiful than the mysticism that Labatut wraps them in. The first part of the book was the most interesting to me - Haber and WW2 and Prussian Blue. On the later half, I feel like knowing a bit about quantum mechanics made it less interesting. I’m also generally just not as interested in the genius-uncovering-secrets-so-unintuitive-they-drive-him-mad trope, which comes to the fore in the second half.

Still interesting how it mixes fiction and nonfiction, entertaining, taught me some stuff about science history. Glad I read it - thanks for the recommendation Gwin!

title: Meditations
author: Marcus Aurelius
review: Meditative. Cool to see how a emperor a thousand years ago journaled about some of the same stuff I did. “Just don’t worry - what will be will be. Don’t worry about things you can’t change. If God exists than the world is good. If He doesn’t then what are you worrying about. Chill.”

title: The Box: How the Shipping Container Made the World Smaller and the World Economy Bigger
author: Marc Levinson
review: Certainly a history of what it says. I’d like to read more histories like this! I’m struck by how much unions and shipping cartels were able to impede technological and managerial progress. Made me think a lot about the importance of standardization and how business orgs, companies, unions, and governments interact especially in such a capital intensive and public-good ish industry as shipping.

title: The Alchemy of Air: A Jewish Genius, a Doomed Tycoon, and the Scientific Discovery That Fed the World but Fueled the Rise of Hitler
author: Thomas Hager
review:
Thoroughly interesting overview of the development of the Haber-Bosch Process for fixing Ammonia, and also a dual biography of Haber and Bosch themselves.

I didn't know much the book beforehand - here were the most interesting things I learned:
- how close fertilizer production is to gunpowder (chemically very similar)
- Before HB, the best ammonia for fertilizer came from South America - either naturally forming ammonia salts or guano islands. Guano was so valuable that US citizens were granted permission to claim islands with high concentrations of guano as land for the US. Apparently this law is still on the books, so keep your eyes out
- IG Farben was formed as a consortium interest of German chemical companies
- BASF, the company who commercialized the Haber-Bosch process, was a dye company, and in the process of making ammonia they became one of the first huge chemical industrial companies
- How critical ammonia was to war, and how critical BASF production of fertilizer and explosives was to Germany in both world wars
- Haber invented the process and also the gas used in French warfare in ww1. Which was ironically also adapted to kill Jews in concentration camps (Haber was Jewish) . He was considered a war criminal after ww1 because of his development of poison gas

Also gives a good sense of what it was like to be an industrialist in Germany during the rise of the Third Reich - you can see how Bosch a reasonable man tried to toe the line to lobby the Nazis for favorable regulation while also being disgusted with their policies and trying to keep his Jewish employees

title: American Prometheus: The Triumph and Tragedy of J. Robert Oppenheimer
author: Kai Bird
review:
Before reading this, I had a vague feeling that Oppenheimer was fascinating. Read this in anticipation of the biopic Christopher Nolan is making, to be released in 2023.

I think this is one of the best books to learn and think about super important issues like:
- Nuclear war
- Balancing "putting your head down and doing your job" and "thinking about the big-picture impact your work is having on the world"
- Red scare / cancel culture
- The value of science
- The importance of management skills, and the rarity of finding technical experts who are also world-class managers

Some notes:
- The overlap in terms of his decisions around building the atomic bomb and Arjuna's conflict in the Baghavad Gita is so fascinating - the fact that he loved that book feels like something that is written into a character in a novel, not something that happens in real life
- Interesting how much of a better administrator than physicist he seems to have been. He was not quite disciplined enough to be a truly great physicist - had a lot of ideas but didn't follow them through
- This time period is fascinating because you have all these people interacting, Truman, Oppenheimer, Einstein, Godel , von Neumann, Feynman, J Edgar Hoover, Bohr, TS Elliott. Is very jealousy-inspiring for me - I want to connect with tons of great people across different fields
- He knows all this about humanities, speaks many languages, reads French novels, etc., but does all of this make him wise? It seems like he enjoys this all more for the intellectual stimulation, but I can't help but wondering that he on balance doesn't seem to have lead a great life, so did he miss the point of all this great art?
- Thriving communities are so important to development of fields. His moves from hotbed to hotbed: Göttingen. Los Alamos. Berkeley, Institute for Advanced Study
- He’s so feeble seeming but so hardy in sailing and horse riding

I am so so excited for the Nolan movie. Cillian Murphy is Oppie! Matt Damon plays Leslie Groves! Thematically right in his wheelhouse (a tortured man pursuing greatness at great personal cost, shadowy government and military forces, the inexorable laws of physics, smart people confidently explaining complicated topics, and plenty of opportunity for multiple temporalities). It's going to rule

title: The Man from the Future: The Visionary Life of John von Neumann
author: Ananyo Bhattacharya
review:
A fascinating man and time. It has kickstarted what I think will be a trend of me listening to audiobooks about 20th century scientists in the orbit of the atomic bomb.

Some interesting bits:
- JvN didn't know exactly what applications computers would have to math and physics and science when he started building a computer at the Institute for Advanced Study. But he believed that going down that path would be fruitful. A good lesson that the fact that you can't see use cases right now, doesn't always mean technology isn't worth pursuing.
- He had a coalitions-based view of lots of the world. He thought people would generally try to work together and communicate. Bhattacharya speculates this is rooted in his Central European background, and that Nash's different approach to game theoretical problems (assumed that people are less likely to coordinate or communicate) is rooted in his own upbringing. Interesting illustration of how background leads to biases in modelling.
- Hadn't fully appreciated how behind the US was in physics and math before it absorbed all the best German scientists in the 30s and 40s.
- German science departments that were bombed in ww2 had recovered their research output by the 60s. But those that lost staff because of people (esp Jews) fleeing Germany were still subpar in the 80s. Losing staff was 9 times worse than being bombed according to some estimate. Personnel really matter.

title: Thinking In Systems: A Primer
author: Donella H. Meadows
review: A good introduction to systems thinking! Definitely changes how I think about problems. Not the most exciting book, but quite clear and useful.

title: Seeing Like a State: How Certain Schemes to Improve the Human Condition Have Failed
author: James C. Scott
review:
The core idea of this book is that people in positions of power necessarily make simplifications in administering governments, programs, etc. These simplifications are things such as making maps of property ownership, assigning premanent names and measurement standards, monocropping, "scientific forestry management", planned cities, etc. These simplifications:
- give power to central organizations
- often come at the expense of practical local knowledge (often out of disdain for local knowledge)

This is not to say that these simplifications are bad, but that you must understand when to use them and when not to. And you should be aware that while sometimes these schemes are made with good intentions, they always serve to consolidate power.

The first few chapters lay out the core ideas, which are themselves super insightful, convincingly and clearly. I imagine for a lot of people, the best use of time might be reading the first few chapters and skimming the rest, which is mostly illustrative examples of the concepts set up in the begining.

I listened to it as an audio book and found it to be one of a certain type of book that helps me form a lot of connections. The types of issues it made me think about helped me come to realizations about other relatd concepts such as hiring practices at my company, the emotional importance people place on names, people's negative views of progress.

I have also read Against the Grain by Scott, and plan to read more by him in the future.

I also wrote a blog post inspired by the book here: https://www.modelsandmorality.com/blog/sometimes-companies-want-to-stay-blind

title: Making Art in the Twenty-First Century: How Writers, Musicians, and Others are Earning a Living—or Trying to—in the Digital Age
author: William Deresiewicz
review:
My basic two takeaways are:
1. We should talk much more about the role of money and making a living in art, and stop pretending that the "starving artist" is something to aspire to. If we want good art we need professional artists who can make a living from it
2. Artists in the US now have to constantly promote their personal brand, engaging with fans directly. They can't just sit back, put out art, and make enough money on it. Merchandise, subscriptions, work for hire, are all critical.

On thing I wish he explored more is because there are so many more content producers now, many many many of whom don't make any money, the average income per producer will be way less. I think this is a good way in which the internet has broken down barriers. But he often glosses over this fact and talks of average incomes declining, where what we really care about would be something more like "how has the average income of the top 20,000 artists changed over time".

The author is quite cynical and cutting and makes a little too high generalizations or recommendations at times, but you can just disregard those as they pop up because the core of the book is really good. He is also quite dismissive of people pursing art amateurly as a hobby, saying "Take the money that you would've spent on your art hobby and spend it on art that was made by professionals... [that] would make the world a better place, much more so than doing your art."

An interesting quote: a filmmaker wanted to 'film in Ohio and figured that it would be generous, as well as cost-effective, to cast local actors in the supporting roles. But "the lack of talent out there was astounding," he explained". He did find a couple of qualified people, but he was forced to fly in the rest, even for some tiny parts, "just to make sure they could pull their lines off."' People sometimes like to pretend that finding qualified employees from a given background is easy, but it can be really hard.

One sad stat that I liked is that the National Endowment for the Arts budget is less than a third of what the US military spends on bands.

Also a good book for reminding me that my ideas about individuality and purpose and art are extremely tied to the time and place that I live in, and are pretty unusual in the grand scheme of humanity.

And as Tyler Cowen says, although the book doesn't say this explicitly, the lessons here are relevant for all internet creators, not just artists. "If you don’t think of your career itself as a creative product — bye-bye!" (I read the book after seeing it recommended on his blog https://marginalrevolution.com/marginalrevolution/2021/05/what-ive-been-reading-191.html)

title: Led Zeppelin: The Biography
author: Bob Spitz
review:
I think this is an incredible book about the halo effect, the way people justify their own actions and those of their comrades, and the post facto narrative sanitization.

Taken as an organization, Led Zeppelin was evil. I think it’s really hard to argue with that. The romanticisation of the “bad boy rock and roll lifestyle” is wrong. They’re actually just bad, despicable, terrible (some examples below).

The depiction of John Bonham is the most fascinating in the book. It’s a great example of where a “Straussian” reading comes in handy (meaning basically, that there is an important message in the text that the author does not state explicitly). What Bob Spitz says, based on his interviews with friends of Bonham, is that John Bonham was a teddy bear when he was sober, and a monster when he was drunk. What he shows is that John Bonham regularly engaged in monstrous, despicable behavior (as one interviewee says, “he was always drunk”).

He physically assaulted people with no provocation. He once or twice dangled someone by their ankles from the 11th story. He rode motorcycles in hotels, actively sexually pursued middle school girls (as did others in the band). There’s an instance of him grabbing the glasses off someone’s face and stomping on them with no provocation. He defecated in the purse of Page’s girlfriend. He tried to rape a flight attendant.

The contrast between how people talk about Bonzo and how he actually behaved is striking, and a great illustration of how people justify inexcusable actions in their friends. Or just lie to protect their band’s image. And it also illustrates the halo effect - how we want to believe that because someone is great in one area (artistic genius) that they also should be good in others (moral behavior).

Because John Bonham is undoubtedly a great artist. He is my favorite drummer, and Led Zeppelin is one of my favorite bands. Fully realizing how bad they were as people doesn’t really diminish the music for me. And I appreciate how this book taught me to compartmentalize (in a good way) between their behavior as people and their art.

There’s tons of other stuff in this book that’s interesting to me as a fan of the band. I didn’t realize how critically disliked they were at the time. Nor did I appreciate how incredible they were as a live band, which does not come across in YouTube videos. Maybe too much time is spent on the dysfunction of Peter Grant and their label, Swan Song.

I also feel like it helped me understand why Jimmy Page never did much great after LZ - he had a particular sound he wanted to make, and LZ was the perfect vehicle for it. Afterwards it seems like he had sort of achieved what he wanted, in addition to falling about because of drugs and being difficult to work with.

Examples of evil:

The business side of Led Zeppelin, run by manager Peter Grant, was an organized crime organization. Grant or his hired thugs assaulting people all the time - from journalists who wrote bad reviews, to fans making bootleg tapes from concerts, to promoters they weren’t happy with. On one tour a roadie would smash the kneecaps of fans who rushed the stage at concerts. They were paid in cash for concerts so they didn’t pay tax. They had undercover cops confiscate drugs from fans at concerts, which then would be used by the band and crew. They pressured a journalist to fabricate a quote from the mayor of Atlanta saying that a LZ concert was good. And they trafficked in huge amounts of illegal drugs and underage girls.

Statutory rape was extremely common. I think this is commonly known, but sort of glossed over. Spitz mentions members of the band having sex with girls who are 13 or 14. As just one example, Jimmy Page manipulated and had sex with a 14-year-old when he was 29. I would certainly call this rape. (Before she met Page, Peter Grant forced her into a car and told her that if she moved, he’d have her head.)

It seems that many of these encounters were “consensual”, but that seems fairly meaningless to me when the girls are 13. There were certainly cases of unambiguous sexual assault (potentially rape as well though this is not stated explicitly) such as a woman being stripped and beaten with fish, John Bonham attempting unsuccessfully to rape an airline attendant, and a journalist being stripped of her clothes. There was also an instance of a woman being handcuffed in a hotel bathroom - unclear if this was against her will or not.

Studio credits were also designed to get as much money directly the band members as possible without paying credit to others. It’s relatively well-known that LZ routinely recorded what where essentially covers (or original music with nicked lyrics) without giving writing credits to the original songwriters. Production their first album was also credited only to Page even though it was in reality fully co-produced by Glynn Johns.

(In an interview the author says he never spoke to the band members: “They were prepared to speak with me when #MeToo landed, and suddenly they weren’t talking to anyone anymore.”)

title: The Armies of Those I Love
author: Ken Liu
review:
If anyone reading this has listened to this book, I'd love to talk about it!

Beautiful story about stories. I love how it uses the audio medium thematically.

Reminded me of Atlas Shrugged which I did not expect, in how people who are curious and produce public goods are called selfish.

Inspiring on the value of questioning, and individualism. Very cool how it explores the nuances of what it truly means to be selfish vs. true to yourself vs. supporting other people, and progress vs. living in harmony with nature.

title: Half of a Yellow Sun
author: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
review:
Great for learning about Biafra. Really good characters - I liked how it was all from a very elite perspective but it showed how they were like pretty condescending to a lot of the poorer people.

Richard, a white British guy, was very relatable for me in a hold-up-the-mirror-and-see-how-ugly-you-are kind of way re his desperate desire to fit into Nigeria and Biafra

title: Nocturnes: Five Stories of Music and Nightfall
author: Kazuo Ishiguro
review: Lovely stories! What struck me most was the captured feeling of having dreams and potential, and time moves on and maybe you never realized exactly what you thought you would.

title: Alibaba: The House That Jack Ma Built
author: Duncan Clark
review:
Very readable, concise, informative coverage of a super interesting company and person.

Author is a businessperson, not an author, and not Chinese, which means the writing isn’t particularly beautifully written or investigative, and doesn’t have some big overarching theory or take. But it’s very clear.

There are really interesting and thorny ethical questions that pop up in book related to doing business in China. Is it right to make a decision to start a technology company in China, which will help lift millions of people out of poverty, but will require cooperating with a corrupt and oppressive government, and potentially engaging directly in corruption yourself?

It’s very hard to get people to trust buying online.

title: Miracle and Wonder: Conversations with Paul Simon
author: Malcolm Gladwell
review:
Mostly this book is one of my favorite artists ever just talking about his craft. So I love it!

Gladwell and Headlam asks good questions and overall gives the book good structure. A lot of Gladwell’s specific theories are oversimplified (sure Take Me to the Mardi Gras has elements of a lot of genres, but so do many pop songs). Gladwell is also over-wowed by Simon’s longevity (longevity is NOT the hallmark of a great artist) and I think overstates the importance of Queens (tons of other artists, (Beatles, David Byrne, Brian Eno etc.), also feel free to grab from other cultures).

It’s funny how petty Simon is about Garfunkel having sung Bridge over Troubled Water, and interesting how Gladwell kind of seems to take this as a sign of artistic integrity.

title: Project Hail Mary
author: Andy Weir
review:
Very fun space adventure. The main character is a little “cutesey lol I’m so random” and super self-centered to be super enjoyable to read for me - pitched more at middle school readers. But the book isn’t really about him - it’s about the scientific method, the process of figuring things out, and some really cool and well-imaged space phenomenon.

My biggest complaint is that the “nations-of-earth-reacting-to-a-planetary-crisis” chapters feel like second-rate Cixin Liu. I miss the scale that Liu achieves in describing the leaders of earth reacting to impending extinction, the awe he inspires with his descriptions of space, and the philosophical inquiry he inspires into how people ought to, and actually would, react in crisis. And I think this book would be better with those things.


In particular, after reading The Dark Forest, I can't watch Grace so blithely give over the location of Earth and all its knowledge to an alien species without wanting to yell at him. You trust this entire species not to use this information against you?! What if there’s a war? The possibility doesn’t even cross his mind!


I really don’t think middle school science teachers have quite so much encyclopedic knowledge as Weir/Grace seems to think they do.

title: How Do You Live?
author: Genzaburo Yoshino
review:
This book is great for understanding how people 90 years ago conceived of progress and communicated it to young people. I could imagine this book being great for American kids to think about progress, character, ethics. Probably would have rated higher if I were a kid myself, but parts of it were very didactic (every other chapter is "notebook excerpts" from the protagonist's uncle, giving him advice).

More thoughts on how this book relates to progress here: https://www.modelsandmorality.com/blog/how-do-you-live-a-1930s-japanese-ya-book-about-progress

title: The Bhagavad Gita
author: Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa
review: I found it super interesting to read assuming Krishna is like the voice of the establishment, who says “just do your job, do your duty, there’s honor in doing work well.” Misapplying his advice could lead you to doing evil because you never stopped to consider the outcomes of your actions, eg working in engineering on technology that will be used to harm people, but you’re good at your job. Or fighting in an unjust war, but you are a good soldier and it’s not your duty to question.

title: White Noise
author: Don DeLillo
review:
Similar to Infinite Jest, A Visit from the Goon Squad, How Should a Person Be in that it is a smart book about disillusioned educated Americans finding or failing to find meaning in life. I tend to always enjoy these kinds of books. But this one I fee fell off a bit in the second half. Something about how much everyone revolves tangier life around consumerism just didn’t feel quite accurate to me (obviously the book is exaggerating, but the exaggerations didn’t feel super true to life). But I wasn’t around in the 80s, so maybe that’s part of it.

I feel like title of this book is way more important than in most books. The whole book is full of characters bombarding each other and the reader with information, and I wouldn’t have thought to interpret all this as white noise if not for the title.

I read it because Noah Baumbach is adapting it for a movie with Adam Driver, Greta Gerwig, and Andre 3000. Also I know David Foster Wallace was influenced DeLillo which makes sense after reading.

A very funny book. Some of my biggest laughs:
- Fathers of liberal arts school kids described as “something about them suggesting massive insurance coverage.”
- “All his teachers are male, wear rumpled clothes, need haircuts, cough into their armpits. - Together they look like teamster officials assembled to identify the body of a mutilated colleague.”
- “The plan was that after the reading the three of us would meet the Wagon Wheel group at the Dinky Donut, where they would have dessert and we would have dinner. I’d brought along a copy of Mein Kampf for that segment of the evening.”
- “We regarded the little tablets with solemn concern. Then we exchanged a look fraught with implication.”
- '“I hate to be the one who says it, Jack, but there’s something that has to be said.” “What?” “Better you than me.” I nodded gravely. “Why does this have to be said?”'

title: How to Actually Change Your Mind
author: Eliezer Yudkowsky
review:
Has made me better at thinking. What more can you want from a book?

After reading this book I have a much stronger desire to be correct about the things I say and believe, rather than to be comfortable

Biggest rules of thumb I learned:

A perfectly rational mind would not be afraid of changing its beliefs

Visualize what you would do in a world where your most cherished belief might be wrong. This helps make you open to changing your mind, if it turns out to be the fact that your most cherished belief is wrong.

People really don’t like to change their minds. Like really

My judgements about things often come from a vague positive or negative feeling about them (i.e., “mood affiliation”) rather than from actually examining and tallying up the facts

You tend to passively, subconsciously believe what you read, and then your mind subconsciously goes back and disbelieves it if it seems fishy. Which is a reason to avoid unreliable information

Spend 5 minutes with your eyes closed thinking of reasonable alternatives when making medium or decisions

Most importantly: Ask yourself often “What is the core reason I have this belief? If XX changed, would I still believe this?”

title: The Anomaly
author: Hervé Le Tellier
review:
Incredibly gripping. Has truer-to-life-than-expected depiction of an MIT student which I appreciate.

The central concept is very well explored. Each character provides a different angle on how being duplicated could affect your life.

It seems like the book is taking cheap shots at Trump, religion, Colbert, etc. But if it is the case that Victor the in-book author is in fact the author of the book, then all of this is just his own pettiness manifesting, not the author's. Which makes it much better.

Even if that's not the case, an extremely fun book.

title: To the Lighthouse
author: Virginia Woolf
review:
Has lots of passages that I think I will come back to over time.

I think this book captures better than any other I have read, the difficulty in pinning down the meaning of life. You see the characters’ inabilities to make sense of the world - there is not fixed point of view from which you can observe the totality of the truth. Clarity comes for a second, and then is gone. You hate someone one moment, and love them the next. Like the symbolic waves throughout the book, we are constantly subject to fleeting sensory inputs, memories, emotions.

“[D]ivine goodness...covers his treasures in a drench of hail, and so breaks them, so confuses them that it seems impossible that their calm should ever return or that we should ever compose from their fragments a perfect whole or read in the littered pieces the clear words of truth. For our penitence deserves a glimpse only; our toil respite only.”

Edit on 16 December 2021: I'm retroactively bumping this from 4 stars to 5. This book has changed how I think about motivation and meaning. 3 or 4 times a week I find myself thinking in ways that I did not think before reading this book.

title: Memory of Departure
author: Abdulrazak Gurnah
review:
Puts me in the head and shoes of someone with an extremely different life from me.

I can't find a better way to say it than that I come away with a sense of how much life sucks to be in a poor and abusive home. The book is really just full of despicable people through a combination of choice and circumstance. It was very valuable and humbling for me to live in that world for a while.

There's a scene in a hospital towards the end of the book that really shows the helplessness that can come from extreme poverty. A woman who can barely walk is discharged because her bed is needed for someone else. When someone asks what will happen to her, the nurses simply say "Shall we bring her back then?"

Gurnah just won the Nobel Prize in literature. The book isn't good enough that I'm immediately going to read another of his, but it is good enough that I will probably read another in a year or so.

"Our seaside town had been in existence for three centuries before Nairobi had even been though of, I reminded myself. We were trading with China before the railway that gave birth to this conceited works-depot had even been invented."

"'Mama, I didn't mean that it doesn't hurt. Only that if she's determined to destroy herself, then we can't talk her out of it.'"

title: The Handmaid’s Tale (The Handmaid's Tale, #1)
author: Margaret Atwood
review: I did not expect unreliable narration and speaking without speaking to explored so much in this book! Nor have I ever been so tantalized by a game of Scrabble.

title: Against Interpretation and Other Essays
author: Susan Sontag
review:
I really liked some essays, especially Against Interpretation, On Style, The imagination of disaster. About half I skipped - I don't know enough about theater, Marat/Sade/Artaud, or Sartre to understand a lot of the essays.

Overall the book is useful for providing tools for thinking about art.

Cool ideas I got from this book (they may not all be true):
- I usually feel a need to interpret a piece of art when the art itself isn’t doesn’t lead to a super compelling experience. Definitely true for the movies and books I like the most
- you don’t need all this interpretation and irony that postmodernism is full of. Just experience the thing
- think of style as the picture and content as the frame, this as just as true as the reverse
- antipathy to style is antipathy to a particular style
- we notice "stylized" work when the style and content of the work are doing different things.
- we have so much production of information in society, that one major value of criticism can be to help us experience the art more fully as a sensory experience rather than adding layers of interpretation
- the romanticism of suffering comes from Christianity - Christianity identifies suffering with honor and love
- criminal trials can be seen as art in that they help us reach a catharsis
- things rather than people are the locus of power in sci-fi movies
- Camp is about having good taste in your bad taste

title: Nairobi Noir
author: Peter Kimani
review: Each story set in a different neighborhood in Nairobi. Cool to explore sides of the city that I don't normally see, especially the level of stress many people are constantly under because of poverty, crime, corruption. Have Another Roti, The Night Beat, Number Sita, and Mathree were my favorites.

title: The Culture Map: Breaking Through the Invisible Boundaries of Global Business
author: Erin Meyer
review:
Incredibly useful book that’s helped me understand some minor confusions and frustrations I’ve had living in Kenya and working with Kenyans and people from other parts of the world.

I think I would recommend reading this book after you have spent a few months struggling with cultural differences. If I had read it before moving to Kenya I think I would have seen these points as obvious, and not easy to apply to my life. But after having worked in Kenya for 10 months with people from all over the world, this book gave me a good framework to interpret experiences I’ve had (why many people I work with don’t seem to want to be very direct, aren’t as strict about set times, don’t seem to want to engage with their managers).

I read it in the past week and have already applied what I’ve learned from it.

I would take Meyer with a grain of salt every time she ventures into history - I think she oversimplifies the historical reasons for certain cultural norms. For example, she says that the historical cohesion of a determines high context vs low context: Japan is a high context culture because it has been relatively monolithic historically where everyone shares the same context, while the US as a nation of immigrants has to be low context because you can’t assume that everyone in the US shares the same cultural background as you. But Kenya, which is a country of 40+ tribes forced together by arbitrary borders, is also high context. So this explanation for historical cohesion as driving high-low context just doesn’t seem that right to me.

title: Starting Point 1979-1996
author: Hayao Miyazaki
review:
I always think it’s cool to see how much artists focus on the very technical side of their work - especially when the art seems to work like magic it’s cool to see how much craft and technique goes into it. Though I did skip some of the parts that were really technical, or that were about 70s and 80s anime series I haven't seen.

It’s such a laborious process it is to make these movies. There is an interview where he talks about a “Finish inspector” who sleeps like three hours a night and lives in the studio, adjusting colors on cels for a TV show


Miyazaki says “Porco Rosso is designed to be a work that businessmen exhausted from international flights can enjoy even if their minds have been dulled from lack of oxygen.” which hits a little too close to home

title: The Alchemist
author: Paulo Coelho
review:
Cool short allegorical book about the meaning of life!

You could take the story to be arguing that you should follow fate and achieve your destiny, but that just seems so obviously incorrect to me that whether or not that’s what the author means, I just don’t care about that interpretation too much. I took the book to be just much more about following your dreams, trying to do new things, have new experiences, enjoying the journey, and making your own luck. Things that sound trite when I write them out like that, but that really clicked in the book.

There’s also a very interesting examination on the importance of listening to your heart, on knowing yourself.

title: VC: An American History
author: Tom Nicholas
review: Seems to be a good overview of what it says. I didn’t know whaling ventures were early VC, that the Rockefeller family was involved in early VC-type activity, or he important role played by the Small Business Investment Act in 1958.

title: Girl, Woman, Other
author: Bernardine Evaristo
review:
I love a novel told from many characters' perspectives with little-no plot overlap (this, Cloud Atlas, Visit from the Goon Squad). Super funny, fun, thought-provoking.

Helped me understand how much racial / cultural diversity there is in England (13% of UK born abroad - basically the same as the US, ~14%).

Each chapter was told from a new character's perspective, but I never felt like "ah this character is boring - I want to go back to the character from last chapter" because each new character grabs hold of you right away.

Coolest thing about the book is how you see issues examined from multiple angles in sequence (issues like feminism, racial / cultural / national / sexual identity, politics, and most importantly how the characters feel about each other) - I found myself agreeing in turn with each character, even when their views were almost in direct opposition to the previous character's view.

title: Haile Selassie: The Life and Legacy of the Ethiopian Emperor Revered as the Messiah by Rastafarians
author: Charles River Editors
review: Fine for a 2-hour-audiobook overview of Haile Selassie, which is the main thing I wanted. Not particularly insightful or gripping, but has the basic facts. Features way more on northern African military strategy in WW2 than was really necessary.

title: How Asia Works: Success and Failure in the World's Most Dynamic Region
author: Joe Studwell

title: Sula
author: Toni Morrison
review:
Whenever I hear a book is “stream-of-consciousness”, I think “ah that sounds annoying”. But I actually really like it when it’s done well.

The idea that the entire town can use Sula as a scapegoat for their issues is super interesting- they behave better when they perceive her as behaving badly.

The deweys are so good. I wish they were in more books. I feel like A Feast for Crows would be better if it had some more deweys in it.

title: The House of Wisdom: How Arabic Science Saved Ancient Knowledge and Gave Us the Renaissance
author: Jim Al-Khalili
review:
Compellingly makes the case that we should see a straight line from the Golden Age Islamic scholars to the European Renaissance. Very useful for understanding science as a long historical process: The Greeks and Indians figured some stuff out. Persian and Arabic scholars built on that. Europeans built on that.

It seems like China was isolated from this chain - there’s no real discussion of Chinese influence on the Islamic Golden age other than the invention of paper.

Al-Khali is charmingly a physicist and not a historian. He doesn’t try to take an objective stance: diving into the details of the theories of his favorite scientists, referencing specific conversations he’s had with other scientists and historians, and clearly disapproving of the use of religion as a moral framework to guide scientific inquiry.

Interesting fact: One reason that astronomers did astrology - even if they might not have believed in it - was because providing astrological predictions to rulers ensured funding that would allow them to continue their astronomy.

title: The Precipice
author: Toby Ord
review:
Did not read the whole book because I'm familiar with the arguments about the importance of existential risk, as well as with all the risks Ord discusses. It's a very good introduction to these topics.

I wholeheartedly agree with the general thrust of the book: People should be way more concerned about the long-term future of humanity, and actively work to improve our prospects.

This is alarming: Ord says that a typical senior politician reacts to his ideas by expressing worry about existential risk but also a feeling it is above their pay grade. Then Who’s Pay Grade is it on!?

Two things I think Ord gets wrong:
- Enabling future people to live does not have a comparable moral weight to preventing someone now from being killed. Ord may have a nuanced view of this, but he uses an analogy to argue that because we think it's bad when a person dies too young, we should also be worried about humanity going extinct too young, which confuses the matter.
- I think we're closer to the upper limit on what a good human life looks like than Ord does. He says "We get some hint at what is possible during life's best moments: glimpses of raw joy, luminous beauty, soaring love. Moments when we are truly awake. These moments, however brief, point to possible heights of flourishing far beyond the status quo, and far beyond our current comprehension." I don't think these moments he describes are far beyond the comprehension of people living 100,000 years ago, even if the context in which we experience them is very different. The human experience is mostly the same. The only way we would get an extreme increase in the kind of "goodness" Ord is talking about is through a fundamental change in what it means to be human, which I don't accept is a good thing.

title: Reforming the Unreformable: Lessons from Nigeria
author: Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala
review:
Pretty dry and technical book, but interesting if you're interested in what it looks like to try to enact economic and financial reform in a poor country. My version has a Bono quote on the back, which is hilarious to me: How much does Bono know or understand about Nigerian financial reform?

Okonjo-Iweala (was the Finance Minister of Nigeria, now leader of the WTO) brings out the tension that exists between political and financial interests in rich countries and people in Nigeria who don’t want international bodies telling them what to do. And it's not only foreign "western" experts who are technocratic in development. Local experts can be too. So getting political buy-in is important, both from entrenched (and potentially corrupt) political leaders, and from citizens.

title: Klara and the Sun
author: Kazuo Ishiguro
review:
So good. If anyone reading this has read this, we should talk.


Three facts about the humans in the book that are fascinating to me when looked at together:
1. They don't seem to believe in souls. Josie's Father is the most likely candidate, since he's the one rejecting society, but the furthest he gets is to say that hearts are complicated
2. They do seem to believe that humans are still superior to Artificial Friends - they definitely don't treat AFs like humans (but why are humans superior if they don't have souls?)
3. They are incredibly willing to put their trust in Klara's belief that a mysterious force will cure Josie

These people have no coherent view of the their place or purpose in the world, so they have no reason not to believe a robot who tells them "things will just get better."

More generally, the adults in this book have nothing external to themselves that grounds them in life. They don't really care for each other - they are old lovers who hate each other, and Josie's mom is willing to replace her with an artificial look-alike proving that she doesn't care about Josie herself. They don't seem to have any spiritual or metaphysical beliefs. They also don't care about their society, or about getting out in the world and having any experiences. The seem to live basically hedonistic lifestyles, but they're not even good at that. They have no purpose, nothing grounding them, and so they're willing to pin their hopes on any incredibly tenuous chance of hope, because they have no other way to escape loneliness.

title: The Alchemy of Happiness
author: Abu Hamid al-Ghazali
review:
Lots of compelling analogies and stories for understanding how we ought to view our relationship with God.

I found this a very compelling argument for asceticism: The soul is like a well, and the five senses are five spouts that are constantly pouring into it. It’s very hard to tell what the shape of the well is when it is full, so it is useful to shut of the spouts at times, and empty the well, so that you can study it in isolation.

A differentiation between Sufi mysticism (in Al Ghazali’s understanding) and Buddhist mysticism: A Sufi’s end goal is knowledge, not the destruction of knowledge. There really are facts to be known

He views angels as conveying the will of God from the throne (supernatural plane) to the physical world. And they seemingly act through the stars: The elements on earth are under the power of the stars, and the stars are under the power of the angels

It’s very interesting to hear stories of Islamic origin about Jesus and Abraham, since the Biblical stories are so ingrained in me

title: How Should a Person Be?
author: Sheila Heti
review: The type of lonely-lost-person-moving-from-interaction-to-interaction book that I find entertaining, and then at the end I'm not sure if it taught me anything. The relationship between Sheila and Margaux reminds me a lot of Frances Ha

title: No God but God: The Origins, Evolution and Future of Islam
author: Reza Aslan
review:
A very readable introduction to the history and theology of Islam! I'm not in a position to judge how accurate that history and theology is, but I'm told it's good. It's very much aimed at a 21st-century European/American audience who likely associates Islam largely with terrorism and authoritarian regimes.

The vision Aslan sketches at the end of the book about using Islam as a basis for a secularized democracy is compelling. You can have a society based on Islamic principles without being tied to religious practice - just as the US is based on Judeo-Christian principles without being explicitly aligned to any church. You just have to have democratic institutions in place that allow the government to change over time.

I could have had many more chapters on Sufism.

title: It's Our Turn to Eat: The Story of a Kenyan Whistle Blower
author: Michela Wrong
review:
I was NOT able to find this book in any bookstore in Nairobi, though they seemed to carry every other Michela Wrong book. According to the author, this is the most-pirated book in Kenyan history due to it being "deemed 'too hot to handle' by Kenya's Asian booksellers".

A rip-roaring examination of political corruption in Kenya. Most interesting for me were the sections on how World Bank members and international donors ignore blatant corruption, partially because they have a mandate to spend money and need relatively honest-seeming governments to give it to.

I liked this sentence: "Humanitarian organisations may talk about making themselves redundant, but their annual reports rarely boast about offices closed or staff laid off."

And also: "[The UK's] baby-faced foreign and development ministers are probably more familiar with the Arctic Monkeys' back catalogue than with the history of the Mau Mau."

This quote from a Kenyan during the 2007 post-election violence is sobering "What you have to realise is that Kenyans don't really believe in democracy." - this seems to be the sentiment among Kenyans I've talked about politics with.

title: The Price of Peace: Money, Democracy, and the Life of John Maynard Keynes
author: Zachary D. Carter
review:
Great as a history of macroeconomic thought since WWI - doesn't focus at all on Keynes childhood and extends far past his death, focusing on how he formed his ideas and how they have been used over the past century.

Makes the case that Keynes was much more a philosopher and political theorist than "merely" an economist. I come away from the book convinced that I had been thinking of macroeconomics in too much of a "mathematical" way.

And like most people who have schools of thought named after them, Keynes would disagree with a lot of what "Keynesians" profess today - stimulus via military rather than infrastructure investment, devotion to mathematical abstractions like the Philips curve, abstaining from speaking out against war.

title: Mrs. Dalloway
author: Virginia Woolf
review: When you’re in everyone’s head you empathize with everyone

title: The Prosperity Paradox: How Innovation Can Lift Nations Out of Poverty
author: Clayton M. Christensen
review:
Highly readable, seemingly meant for business leaders and entrepreneurs.

Creates a framework for thinking about how to drive prosperity that is easy to grasp, then illustrates how it works with example after example. Understand local problems, create new markets (via “targeting non-consumption”), don’t rely so much on aid (public goods such as infrastructure should be “pulled in” by developing economies rather than “pushed in” from without).

The book is not the most rigorous, so if you are skeptical about the value of for-profit business, it will likely not help. But the book is aimed at businesspeople who are already on board with for-profit business, and trying to convince them to think about how to help those worst off in the world. On those terms I think it’s very successful.

title: The Word for World Is Forest
author: Ursula K. Le Guin
review: Contact with other civilizations, especially a colonizing one, breaks a people out of their customers, reason, and style of living, in ways that are easy to underestimate.

title: Blockchain Chicken Farm: And Other Stories of Tech in China's Countryside
author: Xiaowei Wang
review:
Interesting anecdotes and personal reflections on how technology mediates rural China’s interaction with the rest of the world, from a marxist perspective.

Throughout the book I noted down passages where I thought Wang mischaracterizes certain concepts like “optimization” or “capitalism” (e.g., referring to “our desire to control via optimization” as “a total delusion” when optimization as a business concept has huge benefits, or stating that commoditization is a “fatal flaw” of blockchain when commoditization has been overall valuable for society).

But by the end of the book I was more struck by Wang’s view of finding personal meaning in life than by any point of view on capitalism or technology. Wang says that life’s meaning comes from how “I endlessly define myself”, works hard despite believing “the only thing my time and labor amount to is making rich men richer”, and tries to fill the void by watching Facebook live videos and shopping (even referring to shopping as a religion). All of this is incredibly sad, and I feel that this book helped me understand other people I know who feel this way. I come away from it believing more strongly that people live happier and more purposeful lives with true religion (or something else outside of themselves to give their life meaning outside of their own self-image). Because self-creation and materialism don’t work for most people.

Some interesting points:
- Pigs bite off each other’s tails due to stress in transport. So pig breeders try to breed tails out
- 40-60% of traceable web traffic comes from cloud servers
- As of 2018, 5% of China farming is done with precision agriculture
- Wang makes compelling arguments around shanzhai (knock-off products that don’t respect intellectual property rights) as a rebellion against restrictive IP laws that only help rich countries
- Parents and government in China are worried about Christian roots of Halloween, while in the US lots of Christians are wary of its pagan roots

title: A Collection of Marxist Writings: The Communist Manifesto, Karl Marx’s Wage-Labour and Capital, Friedrich Engels’ Socialism: Utopian and Scientific
author: Karl Marx
review:
Marx relentlessly hammers home two insights that I think are really important: that the structure of society and the psychology of people in it are determined largely by economic relations, and that capital accrues more capital causing economic divergence.

Striking to me how the Manifesto condemns the idea of making the world better for all — the goal is to make it better for the proletariat.

The idea that because profits accrue to capital means that capitalists are being exploitative is tautologically true the way Marx uses the term “exploitation”. And it’s important to remember that people’s lives in the early days of factory work under capitalism were in fact worse than they were before factories were created. But given that people’s lives now are measurably better on most dimensions than they were before capitalism, I don’t think “exploitation” is the right word to describe all labor-capital relations. Is it exploitation if you are better off being exploited than you would be without?

Socialism: Utopian and Scientific was very helpful in understanding Hegelian dialectic. The contradictions between capitalism’s freedom vs. wage serfdom, anarchy of market vs. organized production in factories, socialized production of goods vs. individualized selling.

Engels gives two statements in Socialism: Utopian and Scientific that seem both critical to his arguments, and patently wrong:
- Firstly he claims that capitalists aren’t necessary and can be simply replaced with management. But managers do not fulfill the role of deciding the allocation of societal resources the same way capitalists do. And I think Hayek shows convincingly that there had not (at least at his time of writing) been a satisfactory explication by any socialist as to how the proper resource allocation could be decided on without capitalists
- Secondly, he says that when the state “becomes the real representative of the whole of society, it renders itself unnecessary.” But even a totally representative society would still need the state to do all the main things we want a state to do: build infrastructure, enforce contracts, enforce law, etc.

title: The Old Drift
author: Namwali Serpell
review: Very cool how each of the characters’ has such a different relationship to Zambia, progress, colonialism, revolution, race. The parts about revolution or about normal life are best I think. A little bit slow at times. I think the author references her own book within the continuity of the book on page 519. Introduced me to Zamrock, for which I will be forever grateful.

title: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations
author: Adam Smith
review: Useful to see some assumptions I have about the economy built from the ground up: Value of specialization, hw taxes distort incentives, when liberty should and should not be protected, general arguments for pretty free trade. If I were to read it again, I would probably skip some of the longer digressions rather than forcing my way through all of it to prove that I can.

title: The Sun and Her Flowers
author: Rupi Kaur
review:
Picked it off the shelf at a bookstore on a whim. I’m very glad I didn’t know that Kaur was known as an “Instagram poet” until more than halfway through the book, because (having a very superficial view of Instagram) I think I would unfairly biased myself against it.

The best poems to me were the ones about loss. One of the poems is just one line: “i long to be a lily pad” which I really liked

title: Prelude to Foundation (Foundation, #6)
author: Isaac Asimov
review: Cool worlds, not as much on the details of psychohistory as I wanted, all the characters feel like robots constructed to advance the plot which is a pretty big limitation when the plot is basically just an adventure.

title: The Worldly Philosophers
author: Robert L. Heilbroner
review:
A good overview of some of the important trends in economic thought over time. Seems pretty evenhanded. I think it exaggerates the disagreements between some of the early economists (Smith, Ricardo, Malthus), but this is useful to get a high-level view of what each of them contributed.

Very interesting how Smith, Ricardo, and Malthus all underestimated the extent to which technology would transform society. It seems like of the early economists, Marx had the best grip on this, even if his predictions of what would necessarily arise from those developments (the fall of capitalism) have not yet been borne out in much of the world.

title: Individualism and Economic Order
author: Friedrich A. Hayek
review:
Hayek seems like a great critic to have — in talking about socialism, rather than just saying “all this is foolish”, he instead very clearly articulates the problems a socialist has to answer. It’s an incredibly constructive form of criticism that is able to help his opponents refine their thinking as much as it helps his allies.

I think the overarching theme is that people tend to make simplifying assumptions that lead to intellectual mistakes. People have a warped view about what competition means based on hugely simplified assumptions about equilibrium. People overestimate the ease of creating a functional socialist state based on not understanding just how complicated are the decisions that need to be made about allocating resources. Judges have a simplified view of the moral basis for property rights, so grant patents where they shouldn’t. My overall takeaway is to be more more modest in assuming that we understand complicated societal systems.

title: A Visit from the Goon Squad
author: Jennifer Egan
review:
A super fun book that I think is about the passage of time. I loved reading it -- my only reservation is I’m not sure that it taught me anything new, but maybe with time I’ll realize it did.

Strongly reminiscent of David Foster Wallace – Americans who are largely materially privileged but have tragic family lives, weird near-future corporatized American dystopia, darting forward or backwards time jumps within a chapter, altering textual format between chapters. One chapter written as a news story that seems to be a simultaneous homage / parody of DFW (complete with many and long footnotes, including one on quantum mechanics).

title: The Prince
author: Niccolò Machiavelli
review:
