This book is a cover letter. All of this is written to get the approval and hopefully patronage of the prince he’s writing to, right? Doesn’t seem like we should think these are actually Machiavelli’s moral judgements of princes.

I do highly highly appreciate the separating out of empirical predictions from moral judgement, which from what I’ve read was somewhat novel in political treatises of his time. It’s conducive to clear thinking to be able to separate out your moral judgements from the facts of the matter.

Also interesting: When a prince slaughters in order to obtain his princedom, it’s only a “crime” in Machiavelli’s use of the word if the people he slaughters were nobles or others of high rank whom society would expect him to respect. If he slaughters commoners or the families of conquered nobles, this is not a crime. Because morality was seen as how others view you.

Popes used to be real bad.

title: The Tyranny of Experts: Economists, Dictators, and the Forgotten Rights of the Poor
author: William Easterly
review:
I finally understand what people mean by “technocratic” and “top-down”, and get why those are often bad things. Overall, the book makes an argument for freedom in terms of historical development outcomes (extremely complementary to the argument that Amartya Sen makes based on principles in Development as Freedom, though both authors cover both outcomes and moral principles) by giving evidence that freer societies develop economically better. And where evidence is not so available, he at least shows that there is not much evidence that authoritarian approaches to development do well.

Factors leading people to overestimate the value of top-down approaches range from: foreign policy interests of rich countries, economists’ and consultants’ interest in maintaining their prestige, extreme variance in GDP growth by country and year that can give credence to basically any story, fundamental attribution error that makes us credit individual people with outcomes that have more disperse causes, racism at the time the consensus about technocracy was forming

At times I think he overstates the beauty of markets – it sounds like he loves markets in all circumstances and doesn’t appreciate their harmful effects on e.g., the environment or gentrification.

He also argues that the important axis when talking about development is “collective vs. individual” rather than “government vs. market” or “right vs. left.” Both governments and private forces on the right and left can undermine the rights of the individual. Individual freedom requires both market to allow for economic freedom, and government accountability to allow for political freedom, both of which contribute to economic development.

One tidbit of historical interpretation: Easterly argues that the main reason New York outlawed slavery when the south didn’t, was because slavery didn’t make economic sense in New York (e.g., they don’t grow cotton). I think this is a good lesson for those of us who live in cities and have a tendency to feel superior to those in rural areas.

title: flavor profile
author: Greta Farrell
review:
Very thought-provoking, especially on the ideas of selfishness/selflessness/self-care.

It’s fascinating to read an extremely personal work of art from somebody you know a little bit. The fact that I know the author makes it very hard for me to take an objective stance on how this book would appear to someone who doesn’t know her. Not that I know anything in particular about her that affects my reading. It’s just that having an already-existing perspective on any person affects how you view their work — especially a work that is so much about exploring parts of herself that are in contradiction to the impression she presented to others (“I have to keep up the illusion of perfection/For everyone new I meet.”)

More than any other book I’ve read, this book felt like an author processing their own thoughts and emotions through the work. It captures the feeling that I have when I’ve crystalized a thought or feeling in writing. This might be a bad thing except that most of the poems in which Greta expresses the thoughts and emotions she's captured are interesting and moving. Each poem makes me feel like I understand the author a little bit better, and the whole fits together into a unified view of the author's emotional state (or so it feels -- maybe parts or all of the emotional state are literary constructions! But if so they're very realistic-feeling ones).

I have personally not had deep and emotional experiences with sexual assault, or mental illness, or being selfish to the point of neglecting myself, and I often have a hard time putting myself in the head of people who have. This book has helped me understand a bit more. Her way of exploring these topics is compelling, thoughtful, and even entertaining despite the darkness of the material.

Also I really like the choice of putting titles after the poems rather than before.

title: Snow Country
author: Yasunari Kawabata
review:
Confusing, and on an immediate level I didn't find it very compelling. But it made me want to think more and read more about it, so at some level I did find it compelling.

Part of me thinks that the critics who write about this book are giving Kawabata too much credit for setting a book about a cold person in "snow country". Yes, the setting matches the characters' interiority. And I get that he's using lots of good literary tools like ellipses and "haiku"-like writing, but feel like there's nothing he's really trying to say.

But I want to understand it, and might even re-read it some day, so I think it's great art.

title: The Hidden Girl and Other Stories
author: Ken Liu
review:
Liu focuses on character much more than most sci-fi (or speculative fiction) authors do in short stories. His technical background helps him here — his characters still feel like real people when talking about coding or space flight or nuclear power. His willingness to flesh out the characters with personalities that don’t have an obvious 1:1 symbolic or emotional mapping to the sci-fi elements of the story combined with the unusual level of detail in his worldbuilding make many of these stories feel like the starting points for novels rather than self-contained stories. I’m not sure if this is good or bad, but it means that each story doesn’t have a gut-punch ending where everything comes together on the last page.

In Seven Birthdays characters use analogies from Grimm’s fairytales, Chinese folktales, Roman mythology, the book of Genesis, Paradise Lost, and Buddhist/Hindu cosmology. I found this very funny — Liu probably has all these classic stories spinning around in his head all the time so naturally his characters do too.

Ghost Days, Byzantine Empathy, The Hidden Girl, and Cutting are especially good.

title: To Hold Up the Sky
author: Liu Cixin
review: Lots of cool ideas per page. He uses the scale and strangeness of what is and could be out there in the universe to explore the great achievements of people. I especially liked Mirror and Cloud of Poems

title: Wittgenstein's Poker: The Story of a Ten-Minute Argument Between Two Great Philosophers
author: David Edmonds
review:
I get the sense that the authors are trying to puff up the facts and the gaps in the story to make this confrontation seem more significant and mysterious than it is.

Overall seems decent as a brief biography of Popper and Wittgenstein, and as a reminder about how petty and unreasonable philosophers can be.

title: A Room of One’s Own
author: Virginia Woolf
review: The idea that to create a great work of art you have to focus only on the art rather than what is bothering you, or what people expect you to make, is very interesting. I was confused at times about what was fact and what was fiction even though she tells you at the start that she will be using fiction throughout. She talks about how Jane Austen wrote with her own sentence structures — adapting men’s sentences to better fit the use of a woman. And such beautiful and funny sentences Woolf herself writes!

title: Rhythm of War (The Stormlight Archive, #4)
author: Brandon Sanderson
review: The character arcs in this book seemed like a step down from the previous 3. But we get fabrial science galore, and every scene that contains either Wit, Jasnah, or Taravangian is excellent!

title: On Liberty
author: John Stuart Mill
review:
Mill’s arguments for not only tolerating but actually seeking out expressions of unpopular opinions seem under-appreciated, even by people who think polarization is a problem in the world. He was very worried about assimilation leading to a lack of diversity of ideas and ways of life, and believed strongly in our ability to learn from one another.

“The worst offence of this kind which can be committed by a polemic, is to stigmatize those who hold the contrary opinion as bad and immoral men.”

title: The Souls of Black Folk
author: W.E.B. Du Bois
review:
Du Bois excels at exploring the institutional explanations for the vices perceived freedpeople by whites of his time. In doing this he is surprisingly willing to declare that these vices do exist, but emphasizes that they are driven by centuries of abuse. To accusations of laziness he answers “[t]hey are careless because they have not found that it pays to be careful...they cannot see why they should take unusual pains to make the white man’s land better or to fatten his mule, or save his corn.” The land is “uncared-for and poor” because of the outstretched “shadow-hand of the master’s grand-nephew or cousin or creditor”. The “plaguespot in sexual relations [of] easy marriage and easy separation” stems from slaves being sent from master to master without regard for their family situation.

Because he was writing for a largely white audience, he had to counter the biases he knew his audience had. He speaks of perceived deficiencies of the freedpeople in terms that today sound unsympathetic. He says that while “the Negro must strive… to help himself”, this striving should also be encouraged “by the initiative of the richer and wiser environing group.” Throughout the book he is generally clear on the point that these differences are the result of historical forces, saying that it doesn’t “require any fine-spun theories of racial differences to prove the necessity of such group training after the brains of the race have been knocked out by two hundred and fifty years of assiduous education in submission, carelessness, and stealing.”. But it would be shocking to hear a writer in 2020 write a sentence like “The best of the whites and the best of the Negroes almost never live in anything like close proximity,” or refer to “the moral fibre of a naturally honest and straightforward people.”

Of the Coming of John is a great story even ignoring the insightful racial dynamics and taken as purely about the transformative power of education.

Du Bois may well have anticipated the amount of progress we’ve made in racial justice from his time until today: “We cannot hope, then, in this generation, or for several generations, that the mass of the whites can be brought to assume that close sympathetic and self-sacrificing leadership of the blacks which their present situation so eloquently demands.” We are now ~5 generations from when he wrote this. I’d say the “several” generation lag he anticipates for us white mass is about up.

title: Autobiography By John Stuart Mill
author: John Stuart Mill
review: Fascinating how in the 1800s he was able to be at the forefront of political thought, philosophy, and politics itself -- the world of ideas was simpler then, and depth of knowledge needed to be at the forefront of knowledge was far less. Also interesting how impacted he was by his father, and swayed by his father's views.

title: Global Development: A Cold War History
author: Sara Lorenzini
review: A well-written book about exactly what it says.

title: The Way of Zen
author: Alan W. Watts
review: After reading a this book about it, I think I am much closer to understanding how simple zen is. The explanation of how koans are used (to point towards thinking that confuses categorization with reality) was especially valuable.

title: Notes of a Native Son
author: James Baldwin
review: The most striking ideas to me were those about how often we, humans generally but Americans are of particular interest, create or have presented to us ideals (perhaps positive, perhaps negative, and often positive in intent but negative in outcome) about how things ought to be rather than grappling with them as they are, and about the entwinedness of blacks and whites in America, particularly how important the existence of the other is to each’s idea of themselves. I started the book thinking Baldwin was really quite a cynic, but ended it thinking maybe he was actually just blunt.

title: Educated
author: Tara Westover
review: This book confronted me with how much a person's view of what is "acceptable" is shaped by their experiences. And also with how easy my life has been.

title: Against the Grain: A Deep History of the Earliest States
author: James C. Scott
review:
This book convinced me that I was wrong to assume that at the time that life under the earliest states in human history was better than life as a “barbarian.” And I have been wrong to view the move from hunting and gathering to agriculture as an all-around positive development.

It makes sense that we have a tendency to overrate the value of states, because over the past 200 years we have seen a massive increase in human quality of life that is largely due to forces like science, medicine, infrastructure, literacy, and education, which are reliant on a society with a state-drive rule of law. Meaning we associate states with “progress.” Additionally, states receive a larger emphasis in our telling of history both because ancient states tend to leave a much larger archaeological footprint than non-state peoples, and because it is in the interest of people today to draw out connections between our states and ancient states. This book is a great corrective to these tendencies.

title: Dawnshard (The Stormlight Archive, #3.5)
author: Brandon Sanderson
review:
I just love it when a new piece of magic is introduced in a fantasy book that makes me think "ah, well this doesn't really make sense when you consider the effect of inertial reference frames of the two parties, but oh well it's just a fantasy book" and then on the next page I encounter a sentence like "You see both of these hoops in the same frame of reference so they act together."

Brandon Sanderson just doesn't make obvious mistakes, not in his worldbuilding, not in his magic systems, not in his characters, not in his plots. And if you see something that seems like a mistake, it's probably a set up for a plot point on the next chapter, or book, or series.

And while I love the Stormlight Archive and the Cosmere more broadly, this book does have a bit of the energy of a an end-credits Marvel scene. We have more magic to uncover, more characters to remember, more tantalizing hints about the metaphysics of this series-spanning universe to much on. The volume and complexity of it all is nearly impossible to track, and even when you think you know it all, 10 seconds of browsing an online forum will make you realize that of course the disreputable apothecarist from page 739 of Stormlight#4 is the chimneysweep from the The Emperor's Soul - after all they both wear a floppy hat - which means that the sweep must also have written the chapter headings to Alloy of Law because the barber and the headings both use the word "berserk", and should you really be on this forum if you didn't notice that on your own?

But that's the price you pay in exchange for a carefully-charted 40-year, 30+ book epic fantasy meta-series.

title: What's Your Decision?: How to Make Choices with Confidence and Clarity: An Ignatian Approach to Decision Making
author: J. Michael Sparough
review: Easy to read, and very helpful in understanding a Jesuit, and more broadly Catholic and Christian, viewpoint of decision-making, even if not very convincing that this is the right viewpoint. If you are questioning whether or not God speaks to you directly, this book will not help you because it takes as a given that God does.

title: Dreamland: The True Tale of America's Opiate Epidemic
author: Sam Quinones
review: A book that made me realize how strong and futile the desire is to find a single source of blame for super complex problems. Also about the power of cutting out the middle-man, just-in-time delivery, and good management. And finally, and maybe most of all for me, how important and difficult it is for institutions (state agencies, Veteran’s Health Administration, JCAHO, etc.) to have the right data, the right evidence, and the right insights to create the right policies.

title: The Dispossessed: An Ambiguous Utopia
author: Ursula K. Le Guin
review:
Le Guin explores what it could mean to live in a lawless, possessionless, governmentless society on a harsh planet, positing that its people 1. could adhere to a strict enough moral code to make such a society materially survive, if not thrive, and 2. would be truly free, each individual required to do only what she/he required of her/himself. I have empirical doubts about 1., but that's why fiction exists! Because 2. is a really interesting idea and I’m glad to have read a book that explores that idea so well.

There are strong and interesting parallels with Atlas Shrugged, strong and interesting enough that someone wrote a thesis comparing the two! https://dspace.library.uu.nl/handle/1874/240766

I haven't read the thesis yet, but here is my quick compare and even quicker contrast:

Both works have a brilliant idealistic rebel founding a new utopia focused on the value of the individual. The heroes of both novels are stunned by the extent to which unskilled and unthoughtful people can wield their power to thwart the skilled and thoughtful. You could easily imagine Hank Rearden (one of the heroes of Atlas Shrugged) having thoughts “He was therefore certain, by now, that his radical and unqualified will to create was, in Odonian terms, its own justification. His sense of primary responsibility towards his work did not cut him off from his fellows, from his society, as he had thought. It engaged with them absolutely.”

On the other hand, “profiteer” would be the highest compliment you could give to Rearden, and the basest insult you could hurl at Shevek (the hero of The Dispossessed).

title: The Argumentative Indian: Writings on Indian History, Culture and Identity
author: Amartya Sen
review:
Among many things this book does well is that it dismantles the concept that democracy and rational inquiry are characteristically "western" ideas. As an American trying to come to terms with the idea that some of my deeply-held beliefs about "the right way to go about thinking and acting" might be tied to an ethnocentric view of the world, it was a relief to be convinced that Indian democracy can just as easily be seen as a continuation of ancient Indian dialectical traditions as an adoption of a British system, and that the Moghul emperor Akbar promulgated "the pursuit of reason" over "reliance on tradition" before the European Enlightenment had even begun. This does not mean that the ideals democracy and rational inquiry are necessarily the right ones, but it does mean that they are not simply the tools of an elite European/American ruling class.

This is the type thing Sen does really well: Show that the simple narratives often muddle more than they clarify. This is a book about India, but it is also a book about how to think and to argue (and isn't thinking really just arguing with yourself?). In reading this book I learned about the the culture, history, and identity in India in particular, as well as how to approach these topics more broadly.

Sen finds an impressive number of different ways to show that Indian culture is not monolithic, Indian history is not primarily Hindu, and that a proper understanding of Indian identity should embrace India's dialectical (one might say argumentative) tradition. In the 16 essays contained here, he looks at India through many different lenses. He examines the many different calendars used by different groups in India. He explores depictions of India in the west, and how those depictions affect both western and Indian views of Indian-ness. He takes any opportunity he can to bring up the fact that emperor Akbar sponsored inquiry into diverse religious and cultural modes of thought.

In all of these examinations, he refuses to simplify complicated issues. He says again and again in many different ways that India is a complicated place, and pushes against views of India as "primarily X", whether X is Hindu, or mystical, or male-dominated. Sen teaches the reader not to accept over-simplified and easy-to-understand explanations about India, culture, history, and identity, but to look for and embrace the challenging complexities of truth that lead us to a better understanding of the world.

title: A History of the Bible: The Story of the World's Most Influential Book
author: John Barton
review: Incredibly valuable context on a book that is surrounded by so much belief, both good and bad. Makes a great case for viewing the Bible as a collection of at times contradictory documents, rather than as a cohesive narrative of salvation.

title: Kitchen
author: Banana Yoshimoto
review: Certain kinds of good books are very grounding for me, letting me live inside the minds of people in the world who live lives just like mine. There is a scene in this book where a character stands in the cold, looking out at the sea, with a hot can of coffee in their pocket, not thinking about anything in particular. I really liked this scene.

title: The Left Hand of Darkness
author: Ursula K. Le Guin
review: I read this book as being about how love for humanity as a whole is shaped by, and possibly even dependent on, love for particular other people. By creating a society where gender as we know it does not exist, Le Guin is able to focus on an imagined kind of personal relationship that has none of the gender dynamics that our relationships have in the real world.

title: Change Agent: A Life Dedicated to Creating Wealth for Minorities
author: James H. Lowry
review: Easy-to-read account of a very interesting life. Lowry takes advantage of every chance to list the accomplishments of the black businesspeople he’s worked with, leaving me with both an appreciation of their achievements and the obstacles they faced. He believes that business and entrepreneurial dynamism can lead us to a more racially just world, which was a valuable perspective for me to have as a contrast to much of the more revolutionary anti-racist writing that I've seen.

title: The Brothers Karamazov
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
review:
It took me 2 years to read it, so I honestly don't remember the beginning of it that well at all. I found a lot of it to be a slog, and was disappointed at Dostoevsky's psychological analysis that I've heard so much about. Sure we probe the depths of Mitya's soul, but he doesn't behave like any human being I've ever met. So I don't feel like I understand very much about the real world any better.

The trial is incredibly compelling though, and the last three pages are so terrific enough to make me think that maybe I'll pick up the book again in 10 years and it will click with me.

title: The Decadent Society: How We Became the Victims of Our Own Success
author: Ross Douthat
review: “Decadence” is an interesting view through which to look at American culture and politics, but more in a "hmm that's an interesting way to look at things" sort of way, rather than a "aha, this gives me such great insight into the past causes and future implications of our current situation" sort of way. The discussion of declining birth rates is alarming. I like the idea that the western culture and ideology could be transformed by Islam, even though that doesn't seem too likely to me.

title: The Complacent Class: The Self-Defeating Quest for the American Dream
author: Tyler Cowen
review:
Cowen makes a compelling case that technological innovation and social innovation and political competency have slowed down dramatically over the past 30 years, that individuals are largely okay with this, and that our institutions make it difficult to change this. This complacency has benefits such as increased safety and increased ability to satisfy certain kinds of preferences (like cheap access to nearly unlimited movies, books, and music), and makes sense for individuals in the short-term. But in the long-term it means that we will improve less as a society, making life worse for people down the line.

Cowen makes some of his points by leaning on his own intuition for how society has changed (e.g., when he says that the U.S. is more segregated in terms of “overall feel”). But these intuitive judgement are important to making his arguments mentally sticky, and I believe that he has both the statistics and the credentials as a generally open-minded devourer of cultural information to back up these sorts of claims. In fact I think that what is jarring is not that he leans on intuition when making arguments, but that he is so much more open about the cases where he does this than are other social science authors.

The book was published in 2016, and two 2020 issues jumped out to me after reading the book:
1. If you accept this account of complacency, it's very predictable that we would be terribly-prepared for something like COVID-19. Cowen writes “At some point this country will face an immediate crisis, and there won’t quite be the resources or more fundamentally the flexibility, to handle it...Building good institutions and capabilities very quickly is no longer something the American public sector is very good at.” And “As soon as Americans have to rely on their government to do something new and concrete — whether at home or in the realm of foreign policy or public health or the environment — low levels of trust will make that more difficult.” All this, unfortunately, checks out as we've seen.
2. Cowen calls out the civil unrest in Ferguson and Baltimore as potential signs that change is coming - that people are truly acting out their frustration instead of simply voicing it online. The protests and riots we’ve seen this summer in the aftermath of George Floyd’s killing are a stronger sign that at the very least complacency with racial injustice may be on its way out.

author: Liu Cixin

title: The Geography of Insight: The Sciences, the Humanities, How they Differ, Why They Matter
author: Richard Foley
review:
Overall very insightful on how the sciences and humanities approach the project of learning differently (tldr science is more interested in general rules than humanities, humanities values the perspective of individual people and science doesn’t, science avoids being prescriptive while humanities are both descriptive and prescriptive, and science contributes to a somewhat linear advancement in knowledge while in humanities it’s fine to have many different opinions that may never be resolved).

It ends with a chapter pleading for intellectual humility and maybe it should be a law that every non-fiction book has to end with such a chapter. Written from a very western perspective — not bad in itself but it would be very interesting to read a book written from a non-western or culturally comparative perspective about the different methods humanity uses to learn about the world and itself.

title: Convenience Store Woman
author: Sayaka Murata
review: A great exploration of what it means to have something in your life that gives you purpose and the absurdity of our need to understand each other's motivations. It also made me laugh out loud at least three times.

title: Light and Dark: A Novel (Weatherhead Books on Asia)
author: Natsume Sōseki
review:
My main takeaway is that refusing to be honest with yourself can hurt everyone around you. Also that bluffing that you already know somebody else's secret is not a good way to get them to reveal that secret.

Thanks Nadine for the recommendation!

title: American Gods: Tenth Anniversary (American Gods, #1)
author: Neil Gaiman
review: Like Percy Jackson for adults but not as good.

title: Decolonizing Wealth: Indigenous Wisdom to Heal Divides and Restore Balance
author: Edgar Villanueva
review: Contains engaging and illuminating stories about the world of philanthropy from the perspective of insiders who are members of historically oppressed groups. Very good arguments on how philanthropy is complacent and out of touch — less convincing on the moral arguments where Villanueva seems to assume the reader believes in the a priori value of collective rights.

title: Racial Justice and the Catholic Church
author: Bryan N. Massingale
review: The “and” instead of “in” in the title is significant: Racial justice and the Catholic church in America are pretty separate concepts because of how little the church in America has said about racial justice. Mastingale makes very compelling points about how the ideas of conversion and baptism in Christianity give us a way to understand opening our eyes to the racism in the world, and finding redemption for past evils. He also writes convincingly about what the African American experience has to offer the Catholic church: A sense of hope, the power of lament, the beauty of struggle.

title: Mengzi: With Selections from Traditional Commentaries (Hackett Classics)
author: Mencius
review: Very instructive, pretty readable, great commentaries both ancient and from the editor

title: Between the World and Me
author: Ta-Nehisi Coates
review: Very compelling on the need to struggle to find the truth, and not give into the dream. But a lot of the book relies heavily on Coates's metaphysical beliefs, which are very unclear. If each person is only their body and nothing more, then how can it be that a cop killing someone is acting as a force of nature, the manifestation of collective will, rather than as an individual?

title: Very Important People: Status and Beauty in the Global Party Circuit
author: Ashley Mears
review: I don't think I really understood how deeply beauty mattered in society before reading this. It's a fascinating look into the psychology of party promoters, "girls", and wealthy partiers and made me think hard about the participation of rush hostesses in my fraternity's rush (on the whole it made me proud of how my fraternity conducted ourselves).

title: Never Let Me Go
author: Kazuo Ishiguro
review: So many ideas woven beautifully together - the reliability of memory, the effervescence and fragility of personal relationships, classism, and our ability to deceive ourselves by just not thinking too hard or speaking too directly.

title: A Gentleman in Moscow
author: Amor Towles
review: Characters that felt like they were my friends, and prose that felt both playful and wise.

title: Vagabonds
author: Hao Jingfang
review: Fascinating world that I wish was explained better, very cool ideas that are explored pretty well, characters feel incoherent.

author: Sven Beckert
review: Perfect if you want to understand some of the systems (like capitalism) that created the world we live in now.

author: Alex Haley
review: Epic, eye-opening, surprising, gripping, compelling and engaging characters, including one named "Chicken George". What more could you want?
